title: Modern Radiotherapy for Axial Giant Cell Tumor of Bone: Impact of Gross Disease at Treatment Initiation.
abstract: Objectives To evaluate outcomes of modern radiotherapy (RT) for giant cell tumor of bone (GCTB) in anatomically constrained axial sites and to assess the prognostic impact of disease burden at RT initiation. Methods We retrospectively reviewed consecutive patients with pathologically confirmed GCTB of the spine, sacrum, or skull treated with RT between 2006 and 2024 at a single institution. Patients treated with palliative intent and 1 patient lost to follow-up immediately after RT were excluded. Local recurrence-free survival (LRFS) and progression-free survival (PFS) were calculated from RT initiation. Gross disease at RT was defined as a radiographically visible lesion on CT and/or MRI at RT initiation. Survival was estimated using the Kaplan-Meier method and compared by the log-rank test; prognostic factors were explored using univariate analyses. Results Seventeen patients were included (postoperative RT, n=13; salvage RT, n=3; definitive RT, n=1) and treated with 3D-conformal RT (n=9), IMRT (n=3), or proton therapy (n=5). Median follow-up was 79.8 months. The 5-year LRFS and PFS rates were 75.1% and 68.3%, respectively. Four patients experienced local recurrence and 1 developed lung metastasis. Gross disease at RT initiation (n=8) was significantly associated with inferior LRFS (5 y LRFS: 46.9% vs. 100.0% without gross disease; P=0.018). Conclusions In this cohort of axial GCTB treated with modern RT, gross disease at RT initiation was associated with inferior local control. Outcomes appeared more favorable when RT was delivered in the absence of gross disease, suggesting that maximal safe debulking before RT may be relevant in selected anatomically constrained cases.

title: What Is the Natural History and Likelihood of Progression of Indeterminate Pulmonary Nodules in Patients With Extremity Osteosarcoma?
abstract: Background Indeterminate pulmonary nodules are frequently identified on staging chest CT scans in patients with extremity osteosarcoma; however, their malignant potential and prognostic implications remain unclear. Understanding the natural history of indeterminate pulmonary nodules and the prognostic value of individual nodule characteristics is important to help guide surveillance and management decisions. Questions/purposes (1) What proportion of indeterminate pulmonary nodules progress to overt pulmonary metastasis, and what is the median time to progression? (2) Are specific radiographic characteristics-such as size, number, laterality, and calcification-associated with nodule progression or survival? (3) Do patients with indeterminate pulmonary nodules at diagnosis have inferior overall survival compared with patients without pulmonary nodules? Methods We retrospectively reviewed 202 pediatric and adult patients with extremity osteosarcoma treated at a single institution between January 2016 and December 2022, with follow-up until June 2024. At initial presentation, we created three distinct study groups based on baseline high-resolution chest CT findings (0.625-mm slice thickness): group 1, those with indeterminate pulmonary nodules (patients presenting with any number of pulmonary nodules measuring < 10 mm [n = 40]); group 2, those without pulmonary nodules (patients with no detectable lung nodules [n = 146]); and group 3, those with metastasis (patients with pulmonary nodule(s) measuring ≥ 10 mm [n = 16]). Of the 40 patients with indeterminate pulmonary nodules, 58% (23 of 40) were male and 43% (17 of 40) were female, with a median (range) age at presentation of 16 years (7 to 53) High-resolution CT chest images of the indeterminate pulmonary nodule group were independently reviewed by a blinded radiologist, characterizing nodules by size (≤ 5 mm versus 6 to 10 mm), number, distribution, laterality, and calcification. Longitudinal nodule behavior was classified as progressive, regressive, or static. Progression was defined as an increase in size ≥ 1 mm or in number by ≥ 1; while regression was defined as a decrease in size ≥ 1 mm or in number by ≥ 1, with remaining nodules stable. Confirmed pulmonary metastases were defined specifically as any initial baseline indeterminate pulmonary nodule that demonstrated growth to a maximum diameter of > 10 mm during the longitudinal follow-up period. Chest CT scans were done before surgery and at completion of therapy. Thereafter, chest CT scans were performed every 3 months for the first 3 years, every 6 months between years 3 and 5, and annually after the fifth year. Survival outcomes were analyzed using Kaplan-Meier methods, and the association of nodule characteristics with survival was assessed with Cox proportional hazards regression. Results Overall, 58% (23 of 40) of indeterminate pulmonary nodules progressed across the follow-up period, with 25% (10 of 40) of patients developing confirmed pulmonary metastasis; the median (range) time to nodule progression was 19 months (3 to 22). No individual nodule characteristic-including size, number, laterality, or calcification-was associated with progression or survival on multivariate Cox regression analysis. Patients with indeterminate pulmonary nodules had worse 2-year overall survival than patients without metastasis (55% [95% confidence interval (CI) 40% to 71%] versus 76% [95% CI 70% to 83%]; p < 0.001). The median overall survival for patients with indeterminate pulmonary nodules was 27 months (95% CI 19 to 36). Conclusion Our study showed an association with indeterminate pulmonary nodules and survival and suggests that patients who present with indeterminate pulmonary nodules have worse overall survival than those who do not. No individual nodule characteristic was associated with disease progression in our cohort, but we cannot exclude the possibility that with more numbers, an association might be present. Our study suggests that vigilant surveillance is warranted for patients with indeterminate pulmonary nodules until prospective studies with more patients are conducted to better develop evidence-based management and surveillance protocols. Level of evidence Level III, prognostic study.

Confirmed pulmonary metastases were defined specifically as any initial baseline indeterminate pulmonary nodule that demonstrated growth to a maximum diameter of > 10 mm during the longitudinal follow-up period. Chest CT scans were done before surgery and at completion of therapy. Thereafter, chest CT scans were performed every 3 months for the first 3 years, every 6 months between years 3 and 5, and annually after the fifth year. Survival outcomes were analyzed using Kaplan-Meier methods, and the association of nodule characteristics with survival was assessed with Cox proportional hazards regression.

Results

Overall, 58% (23 of 40) of indeterminate pulmonary nodules progressed across the follow-up period, with 25% (10 of 40) of patients developing confirmed pulmonary metastasis; the median (range) time to nodule progression was 19 months (3 to 22). No individual nodule characteristic-including size, number, laterality, or calcification-was associated with progression or survival on multivariate Cox regression analysis. Patients with indeterminate pulmonary nodules had worse 2-year overall survival than patients without metastasis (55% [95% confidence interval (CI) 40% to 71%] versus 76% [95% CI 70% to 83%]; p < 0.001). The median overall survival for patients with indeterminate pulmonary nodules was 27 months (95% CI 19 to 36).

Conclusion

Our study showed an association with indeterminate pulmonary nodules and survival and suggests that patients who present with indeterminate pulmonary nodules have worse overall survival than those who do not. No individual nodule characteristic was associated with disease progression in our cohort, but we cannot exclude the possibility that with more numbers, an association might be present. Our study suggests that vigilant surveillance is warranted for patients with indeterminate pulmonary nodules until prospective studies with more patients are conducted to better develop evidence-based management and surveillance protocols.

Level of evidence

Level III, prognostic study.

title: What Is the Validity of Traction MR Arthrography for Detecting Lesions of the Ligamentous-Fossa-Foveolar Complex in Patients Undergoing Joint-preserving Surgery Through Surgical Hip Dislocation?
abstract: Background Accurate preoperative characterization of intraarticular abnormalities is important when planning hip-preserving surgery in young, active patients. Lesions of the ligamentum teres and the associated acetabular fossa and fovea capitis (forming the ligamentous-fossa-foveolar complex [LFFC]) are frequently observed intraoperatively, although their relationship with hip pain in patients without osteoarthritis remains uncertain. These lesions have received limited attention in preoperative imaging. Questions/purposes (1) What is the intraobserver and interobserver reliability of traction MR arthrography for assessing lesions of the LFFC? (2) What is the diagnostic performance of traction MR arthrography for detecting these lesions compared with intraoperative findings at surgical hip dislocation? Methods Between April 2019 and April 2022, we retrospectively identified 214 hips from a consecutive cohort of patients undergoing surgical hip dislocation at a single tertiary hip preservation center. We performed this surgery for a variety of indications, including for symptomatic femoroacetabular impingement, childhood hip diseases, and for surgically treating acetabular fractures. During this period, preoperative MR arthrography was part of the routine preoperative work-up in all patients for assessment of intraarticular abnormalities, planning for intraoperative instrument and graft needs, and prognostic purposes. MR arthrography results were not considered when choosing surgical approach. Patients without traction MR arthrography were excluded. A total of 70 patients were available for final analysis. Traction MR arthrography served as the index test and intraoperative assessment during surgical hip dislocation as the reference gold standard. The decision to perform surgical hip dislocation was based on the clinical and standard radiographic evaluation and generally not influenced by traction MR arthrography findings. Six observers (three board-certified orthopaedic surgeons with expertise in hip-preserving surgery and three board-certified radiologists with specific expertise in musculoskeletal imaging) independently conducted measurements twice using an adapted version of a previously validated grading system (grade 0, normal; grade I, degeneration; grade II, partial defect; grade III, complete defect); for diagnostic performance, findings were dichotomized as lesion absent (grade 0) or present (grade > 0). Intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs) with 95% confidence interval (CI) were calculated to assess intraobserver reliability and interobserver reproducibility of the adapted grading system. The diagnostic performance of traction MR arthrography for detecting lesions of the LFFC using intraoperative findings as a gold standard was determined by calculating sensitivity, specificity, positive and negative predictive values, accuracy, and positive and negative likelihood ratios. Results Intraobserver reliability ICCs ranged from 0.54 to 0.69 for ligamentum teres lesions, 0.21 to 0.64 for fossa lesions, and 0.30 to 0.64 for fovea lesions. Interobserver reproducibility ranged from 0.71 to 0.84 for fossa lesions, 0.73 to 0.77 for fovea lesions, and 0.78 to 0.79 for ligamentum teres lesions. Traction MR arthrography demonstrated limited diagnostic performance for lesion detection. The sensitivity was 86% for ligamentum teres lesions, 79% for fossa lesions, and 75% for fovea lesions, whereas specificity was low at 32%, 52%, and 50%, respectively. Overall accuracy ranged from 54% to 67%. Conclusion In this cohort of patients undergoing surgical hip dislocation, contrast-enhanced traction MR arthrography demonstrated limited ability to detect and grade lesions of the LFFC preoperatively. Future prospective studies using standardized imaging protocols are needed to determine whether diagnostic performance can be improved. Level of evidence Level III, diagnostic study.

title: Does Inspiratory Lung Volume Help Explain the Association Between Thoracic Deformity and Pulmonary Dysfunction in Adolescent Idiopathic Scoliosis?
abstract: Background Adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (AIS) is often associated with restrictive pulmonary dysfunction, but the mechanistic pathway linking thoracic deformity to impaired lung function remains unclear. Although prior studies have used dynamic MRI to assess lung volumes or chest-wall motion, it remains unclear how MRI-derived lung volumes relate to three-dimensional thoracic deformity and pulmonary function and whether inspiratory lung volume accounts for part of these associations. Questions/purposes (1) What are the pulmonary function and dynamic lung volume characteristics in patients with AIS? (2) What are the spinal and thoracic deformity characteristics in patients with AIS? (3) What are the associations among spinal and thoracic deformity, dynamic lung volume, and pulmonary function? (4) Does total inspiratory lung volume help explain the association between thoracic deformity parameters and pulmonary function? Methods In this retrospective cross-sectional study, all patients were evaluated before surgery and were candidates for surgical correction at the time of study inclusion. Of 183 patients with AIS screened, 62.3% (114) met the inclusion criteria and were included (age range 10 to 18 years; 72.8% [83 of 114] female). All patients underwent standing radiographs, low-dose chest CT, dynamic chest MRI at end inspiration and end expiration, and pulmonary function testing. Patients were classified into two groups: those with restrictive dysfunction (61% [69]) and those with normal pulmonary function (39% [45]). There were no differences between the groups in age, sex, or BMI. Deformity parameters included the main thoracic curve Cobb angle, main thoracic curve rib-vertebral angle difference, space available for lung, posterior hemithoracic symmetry ratio, thoracic rotation, and sagittal diameter. Lung volumes (right, left, total) were reconstructed from MRI. Because several continuous variables were not normally distributed, we used the Mann-Whitney U test to compare the two groups for pulmonary function, lung volumes, and deformity parameters. We assessed correlations among these variables using Spearman analysis. We performed mediation analysis with 5000 bootstrap resamples to evaluate whether inspiratory lung volume helps explain the association between thoracic deformity and pulmonary function. Mediation analysis tested the role of an intermediate factor in the relationship between two variables. Results Data are presented as medians (range) unless otherwise specified. Of the 114 patients, 61% (69) had restrictive ventilatory dysfunction and 39% (45) had normal pulmonary function. Patients with restrictive ventilatory dysfunction had lower percent predicted forced vital capacity (FVC%) (median [range] 68% [36% to 80%] versus 90% [81% to 117%], difference of medians -22 percentage points; p < 0.001) and percent predicted forced expiratory volume in 1 second (FEV1%) (66% [30% to 87%] versus 87% [81% to 106%], difference of medians -21 percentage points; p < 0.001). Total median (range) inspiratory and expiratory lung volumes were also lower (2168 mL [1012 to 4733] versus 2807 mL [1012 to 4716], difference of medians -639 mL; p < 0.001 and 1300 mL [400 to 2899] versus 1604 mL [793 to 3161], difference of medians -304 mL; p = 0.006), but we could not demonstrate a difference in total inspiratory-expiratory volume change (767 mL [185 to 2622] versus 1002 mL [219 to 2889], difference of medians -235 mL; p = 0.32). They also had greater median [range] main thoracic Cobb angles (86° [42° to 121°] versus 54° [41° to 81°], difference of medians 32°; p < 0.001), greater main thoracic rib-vertebral angle differences (52° [16° to 78°] versus 17° [2° to 40°], difference of medians 35°; p < 0.001), and smaller sagittal thoracic diameters (69 mm [38 to 148] versus 88 mm [56 to 144], difference of medians -19 mm; p = 0.04). Because this study did not establish patient-level thresholds for MRI-derived lung volumes or thoracic measurements, the clinical importance of these differences remains uncertain. Greater rib-vertebral asymmetry was associated with lower FVC% and FEV1% (rs = -0.84 and -0.81, respectively; both adjusted p < 0.001), whereas larger total inspiratory lung volume was associated with higher FVC% and FEV1% (rs = 0.65 and 0.59, respectively; both adjusted p < 0.001). Thus, pulmonary function was related to both thoracic shape and inspiratory lung volume, but whether these measurements improve clinical assessment was not evaluated. Total inspiratory lung volume accounted for part of the observed relationship between thoracic deformity and pulmonary function. For FVC%, indirect effects were observed for the main thoracic Cobb angle (-0.15 [95% confidence interval (CI) -0.28 to -0.004]), thoracic rotation (-0.20 [95% CI -0.40 to -0.06]), and sagittal thoracic diameter (0.24 [95% CI 0.12 to 0.36]), with mediation proportions of 38.6%, 26.9%, and 76.6%, respectively; for FEV1%, an indirect effect was observed only for thoracic rotation (-0.16 [95% CI -0.40 to -0.04]; mediation proportion 20.4%). Because all measurements were obtained at one time point, these findings do not show that reduced inspiratory lung volume causes poorer pulmonary function. Conclusion In patients with AIS, greater thoracic deformity was associated with smaller lung volumes and poorer pulmonary function. Mediation analysis suggested that total inspiratory lung volume partly accounted for the association between thoracic deformity and pulmonary function. As a radiation-free imaging modality, dynamic MRI may complement radiographic deformity assessment and routine pulmonary function testing by quantifying inspiratory and expiratory lung volumes across the respiratory cycle. Prospective longitudinal validation using posture-matched imaging and pulmonary function testing, including postoperative follow-up, is needed to determine whether these measurements improve clinical assessment and treatment planning. Level of evidence Level III, prognostic study.

title: Histopathological Patterns in Bullous Dermatitis Artefacta: A Retrospective Case Series.
abstract: Background Dermatitis artefacta (DA) is associated with self-harming behaviors, which can be conscious or unconscious. It is characterized by lesions with atypical distributions and geometric patterns, produced by manipulation of the skin through friction, suction, heat, cold, electric current, or chemicals. Diagnosis is challenging, and there are no confirmatory tests, but histology can provide important clues for identifying artificial causes. Objective Our aim was to retrospectively review histological characteristics and anatomopathological patterns in patients with bullous DA. Methods We performed a retrospective chart review of patients with a diagnosis of bullous DA. Patients with self-induced skin diseases related to other psychic causes (such as anxiety, depression, or obsessive-compulsive disorder) were excluded. Fifteen cases were analyzed between 2009 and 2024. Biopsies were submitted to histological analyses using different techniques including hematoxylin-eosin, periodic acid-Schiff, and direct immunofluorescence, with investigation of IgA, IgM, IgG, and C3. Results Histopathology showed 4 main patterns: subepidermal blisters with neutrophils, spongiotic blisters with sparse necrotic keratinocytes, dermoepidermal or mixed cleavage blisters with follicular compromise, and "erythema-multiforme-like" blisters with extensive necrosis. Conclusions Dermatologists are uniquely positioned to diagnose and manage DA. Nevertheless, when clinical diagnosis is inconclusive, recognition of these histopathological patterns may provide valuable diagnostic clues for dermatopathologists evaluating biopsies from patients with suspected DA.

title: Neutrophilic Fixed Drug Eruption Mimicking Neutrophilic Dermatosis: Two Cases, Including Sequential Biopsies Demonstrating Time-Dependent Histopathology.
abstract: Abstract Fixed drug eruption (FDE) is classically a lymphocyte-predominant interface dermatitis, but an early lesion may show a prominent neutrophilic infiltrate that closely simulates a primary neutrophilic dermatosis. We report 2 cases. The first, a 42-year-old woman, developed a multifocal eruption approximately 45 minutes after re-exposure to etoricoxib, recurring at previously affected and new sites. A punch biopsy performed 21 hours after ingestion of the drug showed a basketweave stratum corneum, intense papillary dermal edema with pseudovesiculation, and a superficial and deep infiltrate rich in neutrophils with karyorrhexis, closely resembling Sweet syndrome. Only occasional apoptotic keratinocytes were present within the epidermis, and the marked edema obscured any interface dermatitis, although admixed eosinophils were noted. Clinicopathologic correlation ultimately established the diagnosis of neutrophilic FDE. The second, a 55-year-old man, had an eruption recurring at the same sites after pseudoephedrine. A biopsy of an established lesion 2-3 weeks after ingestion showed classic interface dermatitis with numerous eosinophils and pigment incontinence, whereas one taken from the same region within 24 hours of re-exposure showed a neutrophil-predominant infiltrate with prominent karyorrhexis and only focal interface change. These cases, biopsied at documented time points, support the concept that the neutrophil-rich appearance of FDE represents an early phase in its histopathologic evolution, demonstrate how it can be mistaken for a neutrophilic dermatosis in the absence of adequate clinical history, and show that clinicopathologic correlation and a high index of suspicion are necessary to reliably arrive at the correct diagnosis.

title: Diagnosis and Management of HIV-Associated Colitis.
abstract: A 63-year-old male with a history of untreated HIV presented to the emergency room with acute on chronic watery diarrhea, weight loss, fatigue, fever and chills. His vital signs were within normal limits and his abdomen was soft, nondistended and tender to palpation in 4 quadrants without peritonitis. He did not have leukocytosis on presentation. CD4 count was 310. CT scan showed inflammatory changes in the rectum and sigmoid colon. Comprehensive infectious workup was negative for any pathogens including cytomegalovirus (CMV), cryptosporidium, chlamydia, gonorrhea, C. difficile, cryptococcus, tuberculosis (TB) and herpes simplex virus (HSV). Colonoscopy was performed and showed a continuous area of nonbleeding ulcerated mucosa in the rectum, sigmoid, descending and transverse colon (Fig. 1). Pancolonic biopsies revealed active colitis with focal areas of basal plasmacytosis and crypt branching in left colon, suggestive of acute on chronic colitis and possible ulcerative colitis (UC). Gastroenterology and infectious disease were consulted and patient was started on IV methylprednisolone for presumed UC flare. Over the next few weeks, the patient proceeded to develop melena as well as increased lower abdominal and pelvic pain with intermittent fevers despite IV steroid treatment. The patient was trialed on IV infliximab also without significant improvement. After several weeks of steroid and biologic treatment, he developed increased abdominal pain with tachycardia and hemodynamic instability. His examination was significant for peritonitis with abdominal distension concerning for fulminant colitis. Colorectal surgery was consulted and proceeded to do an emergent total abdominal colectomy and end ileostomy. Intraoperatively he was found to have a small anterior distal rectal perforation. The decision was made to drain this area widely with rectal drain and fecal diversion and start him on IV antibiotic therapy. His final pathology from the index operation showed ulceration and acute colitis. There was no chronic crypt architectural distortion such as crypt dropout, disarray, crypt branching or basal plasmacytosis that are often seen in inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). There was also increased apoptotic bodies and mitoses that were not consistent with IBD. After reviewing the clinical presentation, his disease progression, and final pathology, the treating team diagnosed the patient with HIV-associated colitis.

title: Lower-extremity Deep Vein Thrombosis after Plastic Surgery: Clinical Characteristics and Outcomes in a Retrospective Case Series.
abstract: Background Deep vein thrombosis (DVT) is a significant complication in plastic surgery, particularly affecting the lower extremities. Understanding the associated characteristics can aid in developing effective prevention strategies. Methods We conducted a retrospective, quality improvement-oriented case series of 5 ultrasound-confirmed symptomatic postoperative lower-extremity DVT events after plastic surgery under general anesthesia at a single institution (January 2020-May 2024). Among 39,055 general anesthesia procedures during the study period, de-identified records were reviewed for patient and procedural characteristics, prophylaxis and mobility pathways, duplex ultrasonography confirmation, management, and short-term outcomes. No non-DVT comparator cohort was extracted; analyses were descriptive and not intended for risk-factor inference. One patient with postoperative chest/back pain and transfer for suspected pulmonary embolism without in-hospital lower-extremity DVT confirmation was excluded from the final case series. Results The 5 included cases were clinically heterogeneous and involved complex perioperative settings, including post-massive weight loss body contouring, craniofacial reconstruction with implant use, neurosurgical-related reconstruction, extensive head and neck lesion surgery, and posttraumatic facial reconstruction. All DVTs were confirmed by duplex Doppler ultrasonography, with thrombi involving the posterior tibial, peroneal, or calf muscular veins. Several cases involved prolonged procedures, reoperation for postoperative hematoma, or delayed mobilization. Postoperative anticoagulation was administered in most cases, whereas postoperative mechanical prophylaxis was not consistently documented. Conclusions In a very low-frequency setting, this series highlights potentially actionable prevention gaps-especially postoperative mechanical prophylaxis and mobility disruptions-rather than establishing causal risk factors.

title: Multicenter Study on the Surgical Treatment of Suprascapular Nerve Entrapment Syndrome.
abstract: Background Suprascapular nerve entrapment syndrome is a rare but increasingly recognized cause of shoulder pain and dysfunction, particularly among young or middle-aged men involved in overhead sports or physically demanding occupations. The suprascapular nerve, primarily motor but also containing sensory fibers, may become compressed due to anatomical variations, ossified ligaments, or space-occupying lesions such as paralabral ganglia. Diagnosis is challenging due to nonspecific symptoms and overlapping pathologies and often relies on clinical evaluation supported by electromyography (EMG) and magnetic resonance imaging. Methods Between 2008 and 2018, a total of 10 patients (8 men, 2 women; mean age 31.1 y) with suprascapular nerve entrapment underwent open surgical decompression. All patients experienced chronic shoulder pain unresponsive to conservative treatment. Surgical exposure followed a scapular spine incision, allowing visualization and decompression of the nerve at the suprascapular notch and infraspinatus fossa. Follow-up (mean 15.4 mo) assessed pain (visual analog scale), muscle strength (Medical Research Council Scale), and EMG findings. Results Most patients had delayed diagnosis (mean 7 mo). At follow-up, all but 1 showed significant pain reduction during exertion (mean visual analog scale score from 4.2 to 2.7) and improved strength (mean Medical Research Council Scale score from 2.6 to 4.2). EMG demonstrated normalization in 6 patients, partial recovery in 3, and persistent myogenic changes in 1 case, possibly due to neuralgic amyotrophy. Conclusions Open surgical decompression proved to be an effective treatment for suprascapular nerve entrapment, particularly in cases unresponsive to conservative therapy or associated with secondary compression.

title: Dual-purpose Laparoscopy and Bipedicled Anterolateral Thigh Flap for Abdominal Wall Reconstruction After High-voltage Electrical Burn.
abstract: High-voltage electrical burns involving the abdominal wall pose complex management challenges, including delayed bowel perforation, progressive tissue necrosis, and durable reconstruction in compromised tissue. To our knowledge, no standardized approach has been described that combines visceral surveillance with abdominal wall reconstruction in this setting. We report a case of a 43-year-old man who sustained a 22,000-volt electrical injury with 30% total body surface area burns and a full-thickness lower abdominal wall defect (16 × 13 cm) exposing the intact peritoneum. Triple-contrast computed tomography on day 3 excluded bowel perforation. On day 22, diagnostic laparoscopy was performed for delayed visceral surveillance; in the absence of bowel pathology, intraperitoneal onlay mesh reinforcement was performed during the same procedure. On day 27, a bipedicled anterolateral thigh fasciocutaneous flap was elevated; sequential 10-minute bulldog clamp testing of each perforator produced equivalent reductions in perfusion, prompting a 4-day delay for choke-vessel maturation. On day 31, the flap was re-elevated and transposed, with the fascia lata sutured to the anterior rectus sheath as a second reinforcement layer superficial to the intraperitoneal onlay mesh. At the 6-month follow-up, the patient demonstrated complete wound healing, stable abdominal wall integrity without clinical hernia on physical examination or with Valsalva maneuver, independent ambulation with a below-knee prosthesis, and return to modified work duties. This integrated single-stage laparoscopic approach combining delayed visceral surveillance with definitive abdominal wall reinforcement may inform management of similar injuries.

title: From Failure to Flow: Indocyanine Green Improves Preoperative Mapping for Lymphaticovenular Anastomosis After Negative Contrast-enhanced Ultrasonography.
abstract: Accurate identification of functional lymphatic vessels is essential for lymphaticovenular anastomosis (LVA) but it remains challenging. Contrast-enhanced ultrasound (CEUS) is increasingly used for preoperative mapping; however, failure to detect vessels of adequate caliber often leads to deferral of LVA. We report a case where CEUS indicated no suitable lymphatic vessels intraoperatively, yet a high-quality LVA was successfully performed using preoperative indocyanine green (ICG) lymphography-guided exploration. Preoperative ICG mapping revealed limited linear channels and dermal backflow, guiding targeted incisions. Intraoperatively, functional lymphatic vessels and suitable venules (0.3-0.4 mm) were identified despite failed CEUS-guided localization, and end-to-end anastomosis was completed. Postoperatively, maximal interlimb circumference difference decreased from 2.5 to 1.7 cm, with symptomatic relief. This is the first case demonstrating that when CEUS-guided intraoperative localization fails, individualized ICG findings can guide empirical incisions to identify better lymphatic vessels for LVA. A multimodal approach may improve patient outcomes.

title: Pneumothorax Following Botulinum Neurotoxin Injection for Trapezius Hypertrophy.
abstract: Botulinum neurotoxin (BoNT) injection into the trapezius muscle is increasingly performed for aesthetic contouring. However, iatrogenic pneumothorax has not been previously documented for this cosmetic indication, despite the inherent anatomical risks. We report a 26-year-old woman who developed immediate severe radiating pain during bilateral trapezius BoNT type A (BoNT-A) injections using a 4.8-cm, 25-gauge needle. During the injection, the patient experienced immediate severe radiating pain, followed by pleuritic chest pain and dyspnea within 30 minutes. Computed tomography confirmed a 30% left pneumothorax, effectively ruling out systemic botulism. Subsequent ultrasound revealed a skin-to-pleura distance of only 2.27 cm at the injection site, highlighting the stark mismatch with the 4.8-cm needle used. The patient was managed conservatively with high-flow oxygen, achieving complete clinical and radiographic resolution within 1 month. This case underscores that pneumothorax is a real risk with blind injection techniques and overly long needles. To minimize harm, practitioners should adhere to anatomically defined safe zones, select conservative needle lengths, and utilize ultrasound assistance when necessary, particularly for thin patients.

title: Robot-assisted Deep Inferior Epigastric Perforator Flap Breast Reconstruction: First Reported Case in the Middle East Gulf Region.
abstract: Despite encouraging early outcomes, robot-assisted deep inferior epigastric perforator (DIEP) reconstruction has yet to be widely adopted because of its technical complexity, cost considerations, and limited institutional experience. We report the first robot-assisted DIEP flap breast reconstruction performed in the Middle East Gulf region. A 53-year-old woman with a history of breast cancer, prior irradiation, implant-based reconstruction, and severe capsular contracture underwent robot-assisted DIEP flap reconstruction using a transabdominal preperitoneal approach. Preoperative computed tomography angiography demonstrated a short intramuscular perforator course and nontortuous pedicle anatomy. Robotic pedicle harvest was completed through a 2-cm fascial incision and three 8-mm robotic ports, with a console time of 77 minutes. The flap was successfully transferred without intraoperative complications. Postoperative recovery was uneventful, and the patient was discharged on postoperative day 3. At 5-month follow-up, there was no evidence of flap compromise, abdominal bulge, or hernia. This case demonstrates the technical feasibility of robot-assisted DIEP flap reconstruction in a carefully selected patient and highlights the successful implementation of robotic microsurgical breast reconstruction within a developing regional program. As the first reported robot-assisted DIEP flap reconstruction in the Middle East Gulf region, this report contributes to the growing but still limited global experience with robotic autologous breast reconstruction.

title: Palatal Island Flap With Adjuvant Radiotherapy for Hard Palate Adenoid Cystic Carcinoma: 2-year Outcomes.
abstract: Adenoid cystic carcinoma (ACC) of the minor salivary glands most commonly arises in the hard palate and exhibits perineural invasion, indolent growth, and late recurrence, often requiring multimodal therapy. Reconstruction must restore oronasal separation, speech, and deglutition; data regarding the tolerance of palatal island flaps to postoperative radiotherapy and long-term functional outcomes remain limited. A 35-year-old woman with T1N0M0 ACC of the right hard palate (American Joint Committee on Cancer, 8th edition) underwent wide local excision with partial palatal ostectomy followed by reconstruction using a contralateral palatal island flap. After complete mucosal healing, adjuvant intensity-modulated radiotherapy (66 Gy in 33 fractions) was administered. Two-year outcomes were assessed using Thai-language validated versions of the EORTC QLQ-C30, EORTC QLQ-HN43, FACT-H&N, and UW-QOL questionnaires. Final pathology demonstrated cribriform and tubular ACC with perineural invasion. The tumor approached the medial (0.4 mm) and lateral (1.7 mm) margins, which were close but uninvolved. Acute toxicity consisted of grade 2 donor-site oral mucositis treated with topical triamcinolone. At 2-year follow-up, surveillance with magnetic resonance imaging of the skull base, computed tomography of the chest, and bone scintigraphy demonstrated no evidence of locoregional recurrence or distant metastasis. Speech was fully intelligible on speech-language pathology assessment, the Functional Oral Intake Scale score was 7, and quality-of-life outcomes remained favorable across all instruments. This case suggested that a palatal island flap may tolerate adjuvant radiotherapy when irradiation is delivered after complete flap healing, with favorable oncological, functional, and quality-of-life outcomes at 2 years.

title: Biopsy of Secondary Angiosarcoma Arising in Native Mastectomy Skin of a Reconstructed Breast Without Prior Radiotherapy.
abstract: Secondary breast angiosarcoma usually develops after radiotherapy or in the setting of chronic lymphedema. We report a rare case of non-radiation-associated secondary cutaneous angiosarcoma arising in the native mastectomy skin overlying a reconstructed breast after immediate tissue expander placement and delayed deep inferior epigastric perforator flap reconstruction for breast cancer. The patient's clinical course, imaging, histopathological findings, and treatment were retrospectively reviewed. The clinicopathological features were compared with previously reported cases of angiosarcoma arising after breast reconstruction without radiotherapy before angiosarcoma onset. A 45-year-old woman underwent right mastectomy, axillary dissection, and immediate tissue expander placement for right breast cancer (T2N1M0, stage IIB), followed by delayed deep inferior epigastric perforator flap reconstruction 1 year later. No adjuvant radiotherapy was administered. Three years after the initial breast cancer surgery, progressive purpura and dark violaceous nodules developed in the native mastectomy skin. Skin biopsy confirmed cutaneous angiosarcoma. Histology showed atypical endothelial proliferation forming irregular vascular channels; tumor cells were positive for ETS-related gene and cluster of differentiation 34; the molecular immunology borstel-1 index was approximately 40%; and MYC proto-oncogene expression was observed in 60%-70% of tumor cells. Positron emission tomography-computed tomography showed no distant metastasis. Because the cutaneous disease was diffuse and surgical local control was judged difficult, multimodal treatment with pazopanib and radiotherapy (70 Gy) was initiated, followed by trastuzumab plus paclitaxel for local progression. No distant metastasis was present at the latest follow-up, although local control remained challenging. Persistent or progressive dermatitis-like lesions in postmastectomy breast skin should prompt early biopsy even in patients without prior radiotherapy.

title: A Dual-parameter 3D Assessment of Alveolar Cleft Bone Grafts: Integrating Bone Density and Modified Volumetry.
abstract: Background Alveolar cleft is a discontinuity of the maxillary alveolar process commonly associated with cleft lip and palate, leading to functional and aesthetic impairments. Secondary alveolar bone grafting (SABG) is the standard treatment to restore continuity. However, conventional postoperative evaluation relies solely on volume measurement. Although 3D computed tomography is widely used for this purpose, it ignores the porous, trabecular nature of newly formed bone (NFB), resulting in systematic underestimation of graft volume and incomplete assessment of regeneration. Methods We developed a dual-parameter evaluation method that integrates bone density analysis with a modified 3D volumetric algorithm accounting for trabecular porosity. Preoperative and 6-month postoperative computed tomography scans from 37 patients with unilateral alveolar cleft who underwent autologous SABG were used to construct matched maxillary models. Bone quality was quantified by mean Hounsfield units (HUs), and volumetric accuracy was enhanced by correcting for the porous structure of NFB using Smart Fill technology. Results The conventional Boolean subtraction method yielded a mean NFB ratio of 44.87%. With our Smart Fill-enhanced method, the NFB ratio significantly increased to 55.85% (absolute increase 10.98%, relative increase 24.47%; P < 0.001). The mean bone density of the graft was 483.01 ± 78.11 HU (range: 358.77-614.64 HU), consistent with the quality of trabecular bone. Conclusions By simultaneously assessing the quantity (modified volume) and quality (density) of regenerated bone, this dual-parameter method provides a more accurate postoperative evaluation of SABG outcomes and can assist surgeons in clinical decision-making for alveolar bone repair.

title: Congenital Melanocytic Nevus Mimicking a Coccygeal Pad in the Sacrococcygeal Region.
abstract: Congenital melanocytic nevus (CMN) is a benign melanocytic proliferative lesion that presents at birth or in early infancy. When the lesion extends into the deep dermis or subcutaneous tissue, it can form a mass that is clinically and radiologically indistinguishable from other soft tissue tumors. We report a case of sacrococcygeal CMN mimicking a coccygeal pad. An 18-year-old man presented with a sacrococcygeal mass and tenderness. Magnetic resonance imaging and needle biopsy findings suggested a coccygeal pad. Because of persistent pain and the patient's desire for removal, the mass was excised under general anesthesia with periosteal inclusion, and the resulting 95 × 50 mm defect was reconstructed using a right superior gluteal artery perforator flap. Histopathological examination confirmed CMN without malignant features. The flap survived completely, and the postoperative course was uneventful. Tenderness resolved completely, and no local or symptomatic recurrence was observed at 6 months. CMN should be considered in the differential diagnosis of sacrococcygeal masses, and needle biopsy may be insufficient for diagnosing deeply infiltrating lesions.

title: The Hidden Trap: Tolosa-Hunt Syndrome Masking Entrapped Great Occipital Nerve-A Case of Headache Surgery.
abstract: Headache syndromes may coexist with peripheral nerve entrapment, which can obscure the true pain generator and delay effective treatment. Tolosa-Hunt syndrome is a rare, painful ophthalmoplegia syndrome characterized by unilateral orbital pain and cranial nerve palsy, often showing a marked response to corticosteroids. We report the case of a 56-year-old woman with a long history of migraine who developed recurrent right-sided orbital pain, maxillary pain, and ophthalmoplegia. She was diagnosed with Tolosa-Hunt syndrome by an experienced neurologist after skull magnetic resonance imaging and clinical evaluation. Because steroids and anti-inflammatory treatment produced only partial relief, and because she also had occipital pain with a positive Tinel sign over the greater occipital nerve, occipital neuralgia was suspected. A diagnostic block of the right greater occipital nerve provided partial improvement, after which right-sided surgical decompression of the nerve was performed. At 1-year follow-up, the patient had no residual surgical sensory deficit, no recurrent severe orbital or maxillary pain, and a marked reduction in attack frequency and intensity. Her Migraine Disability Assessment score improved from 18 to 4, and medication use decreased to sporadic use of simple analgesics and triptans. In selected patients, rare headache syndromes may coexist with occult peripheral nerve entrapment. Persistent symptoms despite appropriate medical treatment should prompt reconsideration of the diagnosis and targeted evaluation for occipital neuralgia.

title: Impact of body composition on clinical outcomes in patients with hepatocellular carcinoma: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
abstract: Background Abnormalities in body composition are common in patients with hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC); however, their impact across different treatment modalities remains poorly understood. We systematically reviewed the prognostic value of body composition in patients with HCC, stratified by curative, locoregional, and systemic therapies. Methods Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, we searched PubMed, Embase, the Cochrane Library, and Web of Science (January 2015-March 2025) for studies reporting associations between CT/MRI or bioelectrical impedance analysis (BIA)-assessed body composition and outcomes in HCC. Results Ninety-two studies were included (35 curative, 10 locoregional, 39 systemic, 8 mixed). Sarcopenia prevalence ranged from 6.4% to 62.8% (median study-level prevalence 38%-50% depending on treatment stratum). Sarcopenia independently predicted worse overall survival across all strata: curative (HR 1.52-3.76), locoregional (HR 1.72-2.51), and systemic therapies (HR 1.34-2.20). Sarcopenic obesity conferred the highest risk in the curative setting (HR up to 3.15). In systemic therapy, myosteatosis independently predicted mortality (HR 1.45-2.01), whereas visceral adiposity was protective (HR 0.56-0.66). In a random-effects meta-analysis of 44 studies, sarcopenia was associated with a pooled HR of 1.85 (95% CI 1.75-1.94; I2=0%), with consistent effects across curative (HR 1.86), locoregional (HR 2.10), and systemic strata (HR 1.71). Sarcopenia also predicted recurrence after curative treatment (pooled HR 1.71, 95% CI 1.61-1.82; k=14). Conclusions Sarcopenia predicts mortality in HCC, independently of treatment modality. Visceral adiposity appears detrimental after curative treatment but may be paradoxically protective during systemic therapy. Body composition should be integrated into clinical decision-making in HCC, though a clear consensus on measurement standardization is needed.

title: AASLD EXPO: Liver biopsy.
abstract: Background Liver biopsy is a foundational tool in hepatology, providing direct histologic assessment of hepatic parenchyma. Although noninvasive approaches have substantially reduced the need for biopsy in practice, it continues to play a critical role in diagnosis, staging, and therapeutic decision-making across a broad spectrum of liver disorders. Methods This Expert Practice Opinion (EXPO) document was created by a writing group of subject matter experts appointed by the AASLD Practice Guidelines Committee. Writing group members performed a targeted literature review and created expert opinion statements that were unanimously agreed upon. Results Histopathologic evaluation of the liver is utilized for 3 major indications: (1) to establish a diagnosis, (2) to stage the severity of inflammation and/or fibrosis, and (3) to enhance clinical management of liver disease. Liver biopsy can be performed using a percutaneous, transjugular, or endoscopic ultrasound approach. Percutaneous liver biopsy is used in most patients, though transjugular liver biopsy is often performed in those with ascites or coagulopathy and/or when hepatic venous pressure gradient measurement is desired. Endoscopic ultrasound-guided liver biopsy is particularly attractive when endoscopy to evaluate and treat varices or portal pressure gradient measurement is desired. The different biopsy techniques appear to have similar safety profiles and yield adequate tissue when performed by experts. Liver biopsy has limitations, including sampling variability, interobserver differences in interpretation, and procedural complications. Conclusions Liver biopsy continues to play an essential role in contemporary hepatology practice. Recent advances include the introduction of endoscopic ultrasound liver biopsy. Evolving applications-including the potential for molecular profiling, use of digital pathology, and assessment of therapeutic response-underscore the continued relevance of tissue-based evaluation in precision hepatology.

title: Baveno VI criteria validation and development of a new non-invasive strategy for varices rule-out in patients with HCC (SAPHE-R: Stiffness, ALBI, Platelets, HEpatocellular carcinoma Rule).
abstract: Accuracy of Baveno criteria for avoiding endoscopy in patients with hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is uncertain, and systematic upper gastrointestinal endoscopy (UGE) may not be necessary. We evaluated Baveno VI criteria performance in this population and developed an alternative non-invasive rule to exclude esophagogastric varices of any grade, rather than high-risk varices (HRV). Patients with BCLC 0-C HCC and compensated advanced chronic liver disease (cACLD) from Italian Liver Cancer (ITA.LI.CA) database, with available liver stiffness measurement (LSM), UGE, and blood tests within six months of diagnosis, were included. Independent predictors of varices identified by logistic regression were combined through grid-search to derive a rule-out strategy (SAPHE-R), validated by bootstrap-resampling and in an independent cohort (Vienna). The derivation cohort comprised 598 patients (age, 69 years; male sex, 75.3%; viral etiology, 69.3%; BCLC 0/A, 77.9%; ALBI 1, 54.2%; varices, 33.4%; HRV, 11.2%). Baveno VI criteria missed 8.5% of varices and 6.0% of HRV, sparing 31.1% of UGE. Independent predictors of varices were incorporated into SAPHE-R (LSM≤16 kPa, platelet count ≥160×10⁹/L, ALBI grade 1), which missed 4.0% of varices (HRV 3.0%, spared UGE 17.6%). In the validation cohort (n=149), SAPHE-R missed 4.8% of varices (HRV 3.1%, spared UGE 14.8%). Results remained consistent in sensitivity analyses. In an exploratory analysis, no HVPG-defined CSPH was observed among SAPHE-R rule-out patients (0/22). Baveno VI criteria showed suboptimal performance in patients with HCC and cACLD, whereas SAPHE-R provided a reliable non-invasive strategy to rule out varices, facilitating variceal risk assessment in patients with HCC.

title: A pivotal Phase 2 study of derazantinib for previously-treated, locally advanced or metastatic cholangiocarcinoma with FGFR2 aberrations: FIDES-01.
abstract: Background aims To evaluate safety and efficacy of FGFR1-3 kinase inhibitor derazantinib, in advanced intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma (iCCA) harboring FGFR2 fusions or rearrangements (FGFR2F), mutations (FGFR2M), or amplifications (FGFR2A), previously treated with chemotherapy. Approach results Open-label, non-controlled Phase 2 trial. Patients with advanced iCCA, ≥1 prior chemotherapy, and FGFR2F (Substudy 1) or FGFR2M/FGFRA (Substudy 2), received once-daily oral derazantinib 300 mg until disease progression, unacceptable toxicity, consent withdrawal or investigator decision to stop. Efficacy was assessed by central radiology review using RECIST v1.1. Primary endpoints were objective response rate (ORR; Substudy 1) and 3-month progression-free survival (PFS3; Substudy 2). Other endpoints were PFS, ORR (Substudy 2), disease control rate (DCR), duration of response (DOR), and overall survival (OS). In Substudy 1, ORR and DCR were 22.3% (23/103 partial responses) and 75.7%, respectively; median (95% CI) PFS was 8.1 (5.5,8.3) months, DOR was 6.5 (4.6,9.2) months, and OS was 17.2 (12.5,22.4) months. In Substudy 2, PFS3 was 63% (27/43), ORR was 9.3% (3 partial, 1 complete response), DCR was 69.8%, and OS was 11.9 (8.4,15.9) months. There were no Grade 4 or 5 drug-related events. FGFR inhibitor class-specific toxicities included drug-related hyperphosphataemia (38%, Grade 3: 3%) and dry eye (36%). Nail disorders (10%, any grade or causality), stomatitis (5%), retinal events (5%), and palmar-plantar erythrodysesthesia (1%) were infrequent. Conclusions In previously chemotherapy treated, FGFR-inhibitor-naïve patients with iCCA harboring FGFR2 fusions, mutations, or amplifications, derazantinib showed clinically meaningful efficacy with durable objective responses, and a manageable safety profile.

title: TRACTION-INDUCED STRUCTURAL FAILURE STATES IN MACULAR HOLE FORMATION REVEALED BY VOLUME-RENDERED SWEPT SOURCE OCT.
abstract: Purpose To analyze macular hole development using three-dimensional visualization of vitreomacular architecture volume-rendered optical coherence tomography (OCT) and to interpret observed anatomical configurations using structural and mechanical principles. Methods This retrospective observational study included eyes with developing macular holes imaged using a swept source OCT. Volumetric data sets of the macula and overlying vitreous were processed with extended dynamic-range processing and rendered to permit three-dimensional visualization of vitreous attachment, deformation, and retinal structural changes. Anatomical configurations were evaluated descriptively. Terminology was applied to denote OCT-based structural failure states without implying a fixed temporal sequence. Results Seventeen eyes of 13 patients were analyzed. Persistent vitreous attachment to the central macula was associated with a range of distinct anatomical configurations, including inner macular cavitation, combined inner cavitation with outer retinal separation, outer macular holes with preserved inner retina, inner lamellar holes, and full-thickness macular holes. Volume rendering demonstrated asymmetric vitreous attachment, catenary-like vitreous geometry, tears in the posterior cortical vitreous, vitreous prolapse, and frequent retinal flaps that were not readily apparent on conventional planar imaging. Longitudinal imaging showed variable transitions between structural configurations associated with changes in vitreous attachment rather than a uniform progression through predefined stages. Conclusion Volume-rendered swept source OCT enables direct visualization of vitreomacular architecture during macular hole development. The observed anatomical configurations are best understood as traction-induced structural failure states of the central macula rather than as a linear temporal staging sequence. This framework better accounts for the diversity, asymmetry, and nonuniform evolution of macular hole morphology observed in vivo.

title: Macular Laceration Following Intravitreal Injection in a Nanophthalmic Eye: Management with Pars Plana Vitrectomy.
abstract: Purpose To report a case of macular laceration following intravitreal injection in a nanophthalmic eye and its surgical management. Methods A nanophthalmic patient presented with visual decline after intravitreal bevacizumab injection. Multimodal imaging demonstrated a full-thickness macular defect, vitreous hemorrhage, and epiretinal membrane (ERM), consistent with suspected needle-induced injury. Following failed medical therapy, 27-gauge pars plana vitrectomy with internal limiting membrane peeling and gas tamponade was performed using modified sclerotomy placement. Results Surgery was successfully completed with treatment of an intraoperative peripheral retinal break. At 3.5 months, visual acuity improved from hand movements to 20/80. Optical coherence tomography confirmed ERM resolution, retinal reattachment, and restoration of macular architecture without cystoid macular edema or uveal effusion. Conclusion Macular laceration is a rare but potentially vision-threatening complication of intravitreal injection, with increased risk in anatomically crowded eyes such as nanophthalmos. Careful surgical planning allows successful vitrectomy with favorable anatomical and visual outcomes in this high-risk population.

title: Presumed Primary CD79B+ Vitreoretinal Lymphoma Mimicking an Ischemia-Like Macular Lesion.
abstract: Purpose To report a case of presumed primary vitreoretinal lymphoma (PVRL) mimicking an ischemia-like macular lesion. Methods Single-patient case report. Results A 74-year-old male patient presented with sudden vision loss up to the hand-motion level in his right eye. Fundus examination revealed a creamy, white-colored, ischemic-appearing macular area excluding the foveal region. Numerous vitreous cells and snowball-like opacities were observed. No relative afferent pupillary defect was evident, and no intraorbital mass or signs of active inflammation were revealed by contrast-enhanced cranial magnetic resonance imaging. Fluorescence angiography revealed a late-phase leopard-spot pattern of hyperfluorescence, whereas optical coherence tomography showed banded subretinal exudates with hyperreflective, vitelliform lesions within the retinal pigment epithelium. Cytological examination of the vitreous was negative for malignant cells. Using next-generation sequencing, the multigene mutation analysis revealed pathogenic CD79B, BTG2, and PIM1 mutations, supporting the diagnosis of PVRL. Twenty-two months later, in response to visual acuity (best-corrected) reduction from 0.5 LogMAR (20/63) at baseline to hand motions, intravitreal methotrexate therapy was initiated in the left eye, which decreased the vitreous cell density. The right eye has since remained stable at 0.2 LogMAR (20/32). Conclusion Presumed PVRL can mimic ischemic-appearing macular lesions and should be considered in the differential diagnosis of atypical ischemic retinal lesions. A thorough diagnostic workup should include multimodal imaging and cranial magnetic resonance imaging. When cytology is inconclusive, molecular genetic testing via NGS becomes a crucial tool, particularly when clinical suspicion remains high.

title: Retinoschisis-Associated Retinal Detachment in Choroideremia: A Surgical Conundrum.
abstract: Purpose To describe a case of retinoschisis-associated retinal detachment (RD) in a patient with genetically confirmed choroideremia and discuss implications for surveillance and surgical management. Methods A case report of a 43-year-old man with genotypically confirmed choroideremia, CHM c.242_245 deletion, who developed rhegmatogenous RD following progression of peripheral retinoschisis. Multimodal imaging, including optical coherence tomography (OCT), B-scan ultrasonography, ultrasound biomicroscopy (UBM), and fundus autofluorescence (AF) were utilized for diagnosis and surgical planning. Results The patient presented with acute visual decline from 20/20 Snellen to 20/100 Snellen in the affected eye following progression of temporal retinoschisis into the fovea. OCT demonstrated schisis cavities with subretinal fluid extending to the fovea. B-scan demonstrated shallow temporal subretinal fluid involving the macula, and UBM was suggestive of multiple small anterior holes within the retinoschisis, though these were not clearly identified on examination with indirect fundoscopy. Surgical repair with a high posterior encircling scleral buckle (#277 tire) with cryopexy achieved foveal reattachment, schisis cavity collapse, and visual recovery to 20/25 Snellen. Conclusions This case represents the first documented retinoschisis-associated RD in choroideremia. Progressive degeneration of the RPE, choroid, and retinal layers may create structural instability predisposing to RD when retinoschisis progresses. This mechanism should theoretically make surgical reattachment challenging. This case highlights the need for risk stratification, close follow-up, and early surgical intervention to prevent reversible vision loss in patients with retinoschisis, RD, and choroideremia.

title: Paracentral Acute Middle Maculopathy Prompting Diagnosis of Severe Aortic Regurgitation and Ascending Aortic Aneurysm.
abstract: Purpose To report a case of paracentral acute middle maculopathy (PAMM) in which persistent paracentral dysfunction prompted cardiovascular investigation and diagnosis of severe aortic regurgitation, reduced ejection fraction, and ascending aortic aneurysm. Methods Longitudinal ophthalmic assessment, multimodal retinal imaging, Humphrey SITA Central 10-2 testing, cardiovascular evaluation, surgical findings, histopathology, and targeted aortopathy genetic testing were reviewed. Results A 44-year-old man presented with intermittent right-eye visual disturbance and persistent paracentral scotoma after non-explanatory neuroimaging. Unaided visual acuity remained 20/25 (6/7.5; approximately 0.10 logMAR) in each eye, intraocular pressure was 16-19 mmHg, and anterior-segment examination was unremarkable. Multimodal imaging supported PAMM, with structural OCT inner retinal/inner nuclear layer involvement and qualitative OCT-A/fluorescein angiographic parafoveal perfusion compromise. The affected inner retinal/inner nuclear layer region decreased from 45 micrometres to 32 micrometres. Right-eye Humphrey SITA Central 10-2 mean deviation worsened from -3.67 dB on 03 March 2020 to -5.19 dB in February 2026 despite unchanged central acuity. Cardiovascular assessment revealed a 5.5-cm ascending aortic aneurysm, severe aortic regurgitation, and left-ventricular ejection fraction of 49%. The patient underwent elective Bentall procedure, with postoperative ejection-fraction improvement to 55%. No postoperative quantitative OCT-A reperfusion claim is made. Conclusion PAMM may warrant systemic cardiovascular assessment when ocular findings do not fully explain persistent paracentral dysfunction. This case supports cautious multidisciplinary evaluation while avoiding unsupported claims of causality, quantitative OCT-A perfusion deficit, or postoperative retinal reperfusion.

title: Retinal manifestations of neglected tropical diseases.
abstract: Purpose of review Neglected tropical diseases (NTDs) are increasingly encountered outside endemic regions due to global migration, international travel, and climate change. This review addresses the timely need for ophthalmologists to recognize the retinal manifestations of NTDs, as these conditions now appear in developed nations where clinicians may have limited prior exposure. Recent findings Modern multimodal imaging has revealed distinct retinal patterns that are frequently seen in NTDs. Dengue and chikungunya present with maculopathy, foveolitis, and retinal hemorrhages. Onchocerciasis causes progressive chorioretinal atrophy and optic nerve involvement leading to vision loss. Neurocysticercosis manifests as subretinal or intravitreal cysts with visible scolices. Schistosomiasis produces chorioretinal granulomas and neuroretinitis. Leishmaniasis presents with posterior uveitis and chorioretinal lesions. African trypanosomiasis demonstrates choroidal infiltrates and retinal vasculitis. Chagas disease shows microvasculopathy with retinal hemorrhages, while leprosy causes chronic uveitis with iris pearls and chorioretinal scarring. Summary Recognition of retinal manifestations is crucial for NTD diagnosis and management. Ophthalmologists must maintain high clinical suspicion based on travel history and systemic symptoms. Collaborative care with infectious disease specialists and utilization of appropriate diagnostic modalities facilitate optimal outcomes and prevent vision loss while addressing broader public health implications.

title: Anterior Segment Ischemia and Neurotrophic Keratopathy Following Ultrasound Cycloplasty in Acute Angle-Closure Glaucoma.
abstract: Ultrasound cycloplasty (UCP) is a minimally invasive, non-incisional glaucoma procedure that has emerged in recent years and is generally associated with few complications. We report a case of a patient with acute angle-closure glaucoma underwent UCP for IOP control. She developed iris neovascularization and neurotrophic keratopathy（NK）at postoperative week 6, followed by hypopyon, flattening of the anterior chamber, and thinning of the peripheral cornea at postoperative week 11, 12, and 14, respectively. We concluded that UCP can lead to anterior segment ischemia (ASI) and NK, which manifest as iris neovascularization, painless corneal epithelial defects, peripheral corneal thinning, hypopyon, and flattening of the anterior chamber. Preoperative screening for high-risk factors is essential before performing UCP.

title: Chorioretinal Scars in Congenital Cytomegalovirus Infection Following Prenatal Valacyclovir Therapy.
abstract: Background Congenital cytomegalovirus infection is the most common congenital infection. Ocular abnormalities affect approximately 14% of symptomatic children, but fewer than 1% of asymptomatic children. Prenatal valacyclovir reduces vertical transmission, but ophthalmic outcomes in exposed infants are poorly described. Methods We describe 2 neonates with congenital cytomegalovirus confirmed by amniotic fluid and urine polymerase chain reaction following first-trimester maternal primary infection. Both mothers received high-dose valacyclovir (8 g daily) from 13 weeks' gestation. Infants underwent neonatal evaluation, including dilated fundus examination and multimodal retinal imaging. Results Maternal treatment continued to 36 weeks in 1 pregnancy and was discontinued at 22 weeks in the other, after amniocentesis. Both infants had macular chorioretinal scarring. Optical coherence tomography demonstrated focal ellipsoid zone disruption in a clinically normal fellow eye in 1 infant. Cranial ultrasonography demonstrated caudothalamic and temporal lobe cysts with lenticulostriate vasculopathy in 1 infant and isolated lenticulostriate vasculopathy in the other. Physical and neurologic examinations, head circumference, full blood count, liver function and auditory brainstem responses were normal in both. Both were classified as symptomatic with central nervous system involvement on the basis of ocular findings and therefore received valganciclovir for a planned 6 months. Retinal findings were stable at 3 months. Conclusions Macular chorioretinal scarring was present in both infants despite otherwise limited clinical findings, and the extent of cranial imaging abnormality did not correspond to ocular involvement. Ophthalmologic examination determined disease classification and management. These observations do not permit conclusions regarding the effect of prenatal valacyclovir on ocular outcome.

title: Group A Streptococcus in an Unexpected Site: Temporal Pyomyositis in 2 Children.
abstract: Background Pyomyositis is an uncommon bacterial infection of skeletal muscle. Group A Streptococcus (GAS) accounts for a smaller proportion of pediatric cases, and temporal muscle involvement is exceptionally rare. Case description We report 2 previously healthy children, a 7-year-old boy and a 6-year-old girl, who presented with acute otitis media (AOM) and painful unilateral temporomandibular swelling. Computed tomography revealed AOM with temporal myositis, complicated by mastoiditis in the first case. Both were treated with intravenous antibiotics, and the first case required drainage and mastoidectomy, with full recovery. GAS was isolated in both cases. Conclusions GAS temporal pyomyositis should be considered in children presenting with AOM and painful temporal swelling. Imaging is crucial for diagnosis and assessment of disease extent. Surgical management should be individualized.

title: Parasitic Infections of the Lacrimal System: A Major Review of Etiology, Clinical Presentation, and Management.
abstract: Purpose Parasitic infections of the lacrimal system are rare and often under-recognized causes of lacrimal pathology. Their clinical presentation frequently mimics more common conditions such as chronic dacryocystitis, leading to diagnostic challenges and delays in appropriate management. This study aims to systematically review the literature on parasitic infections of the lacrimal system and to characterize their etiology, clinical presentation, diagnostic approaches, management strategies, and outcomes. Methods A systematic review was conducted across MEDLINE, Embase, Emcare, and PubMed from inception to March 2026. Studies reporting parasitic infections involving the lacrimal apparatus were included. Data on demographics, clinical presentation, anatomical involvement, causative organisms, diagnostic methods, treatment, and outcomes were extracted. Due to heterogeneity and predominance of case reports and small series, a qualitative descriptive analysis was performed. Results A total of 44 studies comprising 172 cases were included. Rhinosporidium seeberi was the most frequently reported pathogen, accounting for 147 cases (85.5%), followed by Leishmania (8 cases, 4.7%) and Ascaris lumbricoides (7 cases, 4.1%). The lacrimal sac was the most commonly involved site. Clinical presentation was nonspecific, with epiphora and medial canthal swelling predominating. Diagnosis was most often established by histopathology following surgical intervention. Management varied by etiology, with surgical excision commonly used for rhinosporidiosis and mechanical extraction for helminthic infections. Outcomes were generally favorable, although recurrence was reported, particularly in R. seeberi infections. Conclusions Parasitic infections of the lacrimal system are rare but clinically important, with diverse presentations and management approaches. Increased awareness is essential for early diagnosis and appropriate treatment. Further studies with standardized reporting are needed to optimize management strategies.

title: Impact of different intraocular pressures during cataract surgery on retinal perfusion in eyes with diabetic retinopathy: randomized clinical trial.
abstract: Purpose To study the effect of varying preset intraocular pressure (IOP) levels during phacoemulsification on the retinal perfusion using optical coherence tomography angiography (OCTA) in eyes with nonproliferative diabetic retinopathy (NPDR). Setting Iladevi Cataract & IOL Research Centre, Ahmedabad, Gujarat, India. Design Randomized clinical trial. Methods Patients undergoing cataract surgery with NPDR were randomized (1:1) to low (20 mm Hg) and high (55 mm Hg) intraoperative IOP. Primary outcome measure was percentage (%) change in central retinal vessel density (CRVD) on OCTA. Secondary outcome measures included impact on optic nerve perfusion (Flux Index [FI]) on OCTA and comparison of postoperative IOP. Outcome measures were evaluated within 2 hours of surgery, as well as on days 1, 7, and 30 postoperatively. Results 40 eyes (40 patients) were recruited in each group. CRVD increased postoperatively, with a statistically significant increase at 1 week and 1 month in the low (vs high) IOP group. The reduction in perfusion density in the radial peripapillary capillary region did not differ significantly between groups. FI improved postoperatively in both groups, with significant improvement in the low (vs high) IOP group at each follow-up visit. Postoperative IOP was comparable between groups, with a trend toward higher levels in the high IOP group. Conclusions Low IOP (20 mm Hg) during cataract surgery of eyes with preexisting vascular compromise may have a beneficial effect on macular and optic nerve head perfusion, especially in the early postoperative period.

title: Diagnostic Value of Prostate-specific Membrane Antigen Positron Emission Tomography / Magnetic Resonance Imaging in Selected Men with Equivocal Prostate Imaging Reporting and Data System Category 3 Lesion (PANDORA): A Prospective Paired Diagnostic Study.
abstract: Purpose Equivocal Prostate Imaging Reporting and Data System (PI-RADS) category 3 lesions carry an intermediate risk of clinically significant prostate cancer (csPCa). We evaluated the diagnostic value of prostate-specific membrane antigen positron emission tomography/magnetic resonance imaging (PSMA PET/MRI) with [18F]JK-PSMA-7, performed after diagnostic MRI, in biopsy-eligible men with an equivocal PI-RADS category 3 lesion. We hypothesized that PSMA PET-targeted biopsy would detect more csPCa than MRI-targeted biopsy. Materials and methods We conducted a single-center prospective paired diagnostic study from November 2023 to February 2026. Biopsy-eligible men with an equivocal PI-RADS category 3 lesion on diagnostic MRI and ≥1 high-risk feature underwent pre-biopsy PSMA PET/MRI, with positivity defined as a PRIMARY score ≥3, followed by transperineal MRI-targeted, PSMA PET-targeted when positive, and systematic biopsy. The primary outcome was the per-patient csPCa detection rate (International Society of Urological Pathology grade group ≥2 with ≥10% Gleason pattern 4) of PSMA PET-targeted vs MRI-targeted biopsy, assessed with the exact McNemar test. Results Of 83 men assessed, 66 completed PSMA PET/MRI and biopsy. PSMA PET was positive in 21 of 66 (32%). PSMA PET-targeted biopsy detected csPCa in 10 of 66 (15%) vs 4 of 66 (6%) for MRI-targeted biopsy (difference 9%; 95% CI 2%-18%; P = .03). Sensitivity, specificity, and negative predictive value of PSMA PET were 100%, 82%, and 100%. Biopsy would have been avoided in 45 of 66 men (68%) with a negative result, none of whom had csPCa. Conclusions In biopsy-eligible men with an equivocal PI-RADS category 3 lesion, PSMA PET-targeted biopsy detected more csPCa than MRI-targeted biopsy. The high negative predictive value suggests that deferral of biopsy after a negative result merits evaluation in larger multicentre studies.

title: Diagnostic Strategies After Negative Colposcopy in High-Grade Cervical Cytology: A Multicenter Randomized Trial.
abstract: Objectives To compare diagnostic strategies for detecting HSIL or worse (HSIL+) in women with high-grade cytology and negative colposcopy, and to assess whether sequential HPV testing, liquid-based cytology (LBC), and endocervical sampling improve diagnostic safety. Methods This is a multicenter randomized clinical trial conducted at 4 referral centers between 2021 and 2022. Women with ASC-H or worse cytology and negative colposcopy underwent HPV testing and LBC. Participants were randomized to endocervical brushing (EB) or endocervical curettage (ECC). The reference standard was histopathology from excisional procedures or structured follow-up. Diagnostic performance (sensitivity, specificity, predictive values, and accuracy) was calculated for individual tests and predefined combinations (AND ALL and MAJORITY rules). Absolute differences between strategies were analyzed. Invalid results were classified as failures (false negatives or false positives) according to the final diagnosis. Results Among 257 women, 35 cases of HSIL+ were identified. HPV testing showed the highest sensitivity (94.3%) and negative predictive value (98.6%), whereas LBC demonstrated higher specificity (84.9%) and accuracy (84.1%). The combination of HPV and LBC (AND rule) improved specificity to 91.7% with a sensitivity of 77.1%. Adding EB (MAJORITY rule) increased sensitivity to 100% (absolute increase 22.9%) but reduced specificity to 82.3%. ECC showed lower sensitivity (61.1%) and higher inadequacy rates (21.3%). Conclusions In women with high-grade cytology and negative colposcopy, HPV testing followed by LBC provides a balanced diagnostic strategy. The addition of endocervical brushing may increase sensitivity in selected high-risk cases and improve the detection of HSIL+ after negative colposcopy.

title: Optimizing Cochlear Implant Outcomes in Cochlear Nerve Aplasia: The EMPES Protocol (Early Implantation, Modiolar Proximity, and Early Switch-On).
abstract: Objective To evaluate the efficacy of EMPES [Early implantation, Modiolar Proximity (MP), and Early Switch-on] approach in bilateral cochlear nerve (CN) aplasia. Study design Retrospective cohort study. Setting Tertiary referral center. Patients Forty-six children (86 ears) with bilateral CN aplasia underwent cochlear implantation (CI) between 2011 and 2024 at 2 tertiary centers. Intervention For electrophysiological comparison, CI was performed using CI24RE-CA electrodes without pull-back (conventional implantation) or a slim modiolar electrode with pull-back (better MP). For speech outcome comparison, the conventional approach group comprised conventional implantation cases with ≥12-month follow-up, and the EMPES approach group comprised those in the better MP group implanted before 12 months and followed for ≥12 months. Main outcome measures Mechanistic endpoint, intraoperative ECAP positivity; functional endpoint: longitudinal Categories of Auditory Performance (CAP) scores up to 48 months. Results The better MP group showed higher intraoperative ECAP positivity, which translated into better postoperative outcomes. The EMPES approach demonstrated clear superiority in auditory performance up to 12 months [CAP score 3.00 (2.00 to 4.00) vs. 1.50 (1.00 to 2.25); P=0.010], with significantly fewer poor responders (CAP<2) at 1 year, and maintained narrower variability in median CAP scores through 36 months, indicating more stable auditory progress compared with the conventional approach. No clear association was observed between MRI-based CN aplasia severity and either ECAP positivity or audiological outcomes. Conclusions The EMPES approach improves postoperative audiological outcomes during critical language periods and is recommended for bilateral CN aplasia to enhance language development and potentially reduce the need for auditory brainstem implantation.

title: Computed Tomography-Derived Psoas Muscle Quantity, Attenuation, and 1 Year Mortality in Venovenous Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation.
abstract: Computed tomography (CT)-derived skeletal muscle characteristics may provide prognostic information in patients receiving venovenous extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VV ECMO), but the relative contributions of muscle quantity and attenuation remain uncertain. We retrospectively studied adults who received VV ECMO for severe respiratory failure between 2014 and 2023 and underwent abdominal CT within 48 h before ECMO initiation. Psoas muscle index (PMI) and attenuation were measured using an artificial intelligence-based pipeline, and combined PMI-attenuation phenotypes were evaluated for 1 year mortality. Among 92 patients, 53 (57.6%) died within 1 year. In Cox proportional hazards models adjusted for age, sex, and initial Sequential Organ Failure Assessment score and stratified by bridge-to-transplantation status, higher PMI (adjusted hazard ratio [aHR] per standard deviation increase, 0.58; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.41-0.82) and higher attenuation (aHR per 5 Hounsfield unit increase, 0.87; 95% CI, 0.77-0.97) were associated with lower 1 year mortality. When modeled simultaneously, PMI remained significant, whereas attenuation did not. The low PMI/low attenuation phenotype had the highest mortality risk (aHR, 5.30; 95% CI, 2.10-13.34). PMI showed a more robust association with 1 year mortality, while combined PMI-attenuation phenotyping may identify a particularly high-risk subgroup.
