title: Suspected Small Bowel Bleeding: A Single-Center Retrospective Study on Long-Term Prognosis and Predictive Factors.
abstract: Goals We identified prognostic factors for mortality after Suspected small bowel bleeding (SSBB) and evaluated the impact of severe anemia and other clinical factors on patient survival. Background SSBB is characterized by an inability to identify the cause of bleeding despite esophagogastroduodenoscopy and colonoscopy. Study This retrospective observational study included patients aged ≥20 years with SSBB who underwent capsule endoscopy (CE) at Hokkaido University Hospital in Japan from April 2015 to March 2022. Patient characteristics, blood transfusion history, CE results, blood test results, and post-CE mortality events were collected from electronic medical records. Results CE was performed in 99 patients to investigate the causes of SSBB, identifying bleeding sources in 40.4%. Over a median follow-up of 35 months (range: 0 to 94), mortality occurred in 34 cases. The overall 3-year survival rate was 71.1%. Multivariate analysis identified hemoglobin levels <8.0 g/dL [hazard ratio ( HR )=9.75; 95% CI: 1.26-75.15; P =0.003] and end-stage cancer ( HR =4.94; 95% CI: 2.02-12.10; P <0.001) as independent prognostic factors for mortality after CE for SSBB. Even after excluding patients with small bowel tumors and end-stage cancer, hemoglobin levels <8.0 g/dL ( HR =5.07; 95% CI: 1.10-23.03; P =0.037) remained an independent predictor of mortality. The overall 5-year survival rates for patients without small bowel tumors and end-stage cancer in the groups with hemoglobin levels of ≥8.0 g/dL and <8.0 g/dL were 89.0% and 56.8%, respectively. Conclusion Hemoglobin levels <8.0 g/dL significantly predict mortality in patients with SSBB.

title: Parsonage-turner syndrome: a pulmonologist's guide to the forgotten diaphragm.
abstract: Purpose of review Parsonage-Turner syndrome (PTS), or neuralgic amyotrophy, is framed as a shoulder disorder owned by neurology, and that framing has cost pulmonologists patients. Roughly 1 in 13 develops phrenic neuropathy, and many patients referred for unexplained dyspnea, orthopnea, or rapid eye movement (REM)-predominant sleep-disordered breathing have an undiagnosed, treatable inflammatory neuropathy. This review reframes PTS for pulmonologists. Recent findings Three developments have reshaped practice. High-resolution neuromuscular ultrasound and MR neurography now identify the hourglass constrictions and fascicular entwinement of PTS at the bedside, including in the phrenic nerve. COVID-19 infection and SARS-CoV-2 vaccination produced a global cluster, expanding the phenotype toward bilateral and respiratory-predominant disease. Large Dutch cohort data have replaced anecdote with structure: roughly 60% of patients with phrenic involvement recover meaningfully within 2 years, while the remainder respond best to early noninvasive ventilation and, in refractory cases, diaphragmatic plication. Summary Every pulmonologist evaluating unexplained dyspnea, disproportionate orthopnea, or REM-predominant hypopneas should ask one question: was there severe shoulder or neck pain in the weeks before the breathing changed? If yes, screen with upright and supine spirometry and diaphragm ultrasound. The diagnosis is reachable in a single visit, the immunomodulation window is short, and the cost of missing it is years of avoidable disability.

If yes, screen with upright and supine spirometry and diaphragm ultrasound. The diagnosis is reachable in a single visit, the immunomodulation window is short, and the cost of missing it is years of avoidable disability.

title: Clinical curative effect of B-ultrasound-guided minimally invasive percutaneous nephrolithotomy and its influences on stone clearance rate in patients with complex kidney stones.
abstract: This study compares short-term perioperative and early postoperative outcomes of B-ultrasound-guided minimally invasive percutaneous nephrolithotomy (MPCNL) and retroperitoneal laparoscopic pyelolithotomy (RLP) in patients with complex kidney stones. This single-center retrospective observational cohort included 120 eligible patients treated between December 2020 and December 2023. Patients were classified according to the treatment actually received (RLP, n = 60; B-ultrasound-guided MPCNL, n = 60); no random allocation was performed. Outcomes included perioperative indicators, 24-hour visual analog scale pain score, 48-hour inflammatory and renal biomarkers, early ultrasound-defined stone clearance at postoperative day 1, and in-hospital complications. Operation time, intraoperative blood loss, and length of hospital stay were lower in the MPCNL group than in the RLP group (nominal P < .05). Early ultrasound-defined stone clearance was 91.67% (55/60) versus 78.33% (47/60), corresponding to a risk difference of 13.3 percentage points (95% confidence interval [CI] = 0.2-25.6), a risk ratio of 1.17 (95% CI = 1.00-1.36), and a Pearson chi-square P = .041. This comparison did not meet a conservative Bonferroni-adjusted threshold of 0.0042 for 12 reported endpoints. At 24 hours, visual analog scale scores were lower in the MPCNL group, and at 48 hours, inflammatory and renal biomarkers were lower (nominal P < .05). Complications occurred in 2/60 (3.33%) versus 8/60 (13.33%); because of sparse events, Fisher exact test was used (P = .095; risk ratio = 0.25, 95% CI = 0.06-1.13). B-ultrasound-guided MPCNL was associated with more favorable short-term perioperative and biomarker outcomes and a nominally higher early ultrasound-defined clearance rate than RLP. However, the retrospective nonrandomized design, incomplete baseline adjustment, short follow-up, outcome-measurement limitations, and multiple comparisons preclude causal or long-term effectiveness claims. These findings should be considered hypothesis-generating and require confirmation in adequately powered prospective comparative studies.

title: Artificial intelligence empowering the diagnosis and treatment of rotator cuff tears: A systematic review from image optimization to prognosis prediction.
abstract: Background Artificial intelligence (AI) is being developed for image acquisition, quantitative tissue assessment, diagnosis, and clinical prediction in rotator cuff tears. The breadth of this literature and its methodological limitations have not been integrated across the complete care pathway. Methods We searched PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, Scopus, and the Cochrane Library from inception to July 5, 2026 for English-language original studies applying AI to rotator cuff-related reconstruction, segmentation or quantitative imaging, diagnosis or classification, anatomical measurement, or prognosis. Two reviewers screened reports and extracted study, data, model, validation, reference standard, and performance characteristics. Diagnostic accuracy studies were assessed with QUADAS-2 and prediction-model studies with PROBAST. Because clinical tasks, modalities, models, reference standards, and reported metrics were not sufficiently comparable, evidence was synthesized narratively rather than pooled statistically. Results Sixty-six reports were included: 35 diagnostic accuracy or classification studies, 20 segmentation or quantitative imaging studies, 9 prognosis or outcome prediction studies, 1 Magnetic Resonance Imaging reconstruction or image-optimization study, and 1 exploratory unsupervised-phenotyping study. Applications spanned Magnetic Resonance Imaging, radiography, ultrasound, computed tomography, clinical or multimodal data, motion video, and emerging sensing data. QUADAS-2 classified overall risk-of-bias as high in 27/36 diagnostic studies, unclear in 6/36, and low in 3/36. PROBAST classified all 8/8 completed prediction-model studies as high risk-of-bias; 1 protocol without model results was not rated. Promising internal performance was recurrent, but selection methods, imperfect or incompletely described reference standards, limited external validation, small or selected datasets, and analysis-stage weaknesses constrained clinical inference. Conclusion AI has proof-of-concept value across rotator cuff imaging and decision support, but the current evidence does not establish routine clinical readiness or replacement of clinician judgment. Prospective multicenter studies, transparent reference standards, independent external validation, calibration and clinical-utility assessment, and standardized task-specific reporting are required.

title: Cholecystogastric fistula masquerading as gastrointestinal stromal tumour: Unusual presentation of gallbladder adenomyomatosis - a case report.
abstract: Rationale We present the case of gallbladder adenomyomatosis (GA)-induced cholecystogastric fistula (CGF) that mimicked an invasive gastric gastrointestinal stromal tumor (GIST), leading to diagnostic and surgical challenges in an emergency setting. Patient concerns A 71-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with acute abdominal pain and clinical signs of mechanical small-bowel obstruction (SBO). Diagnoses Contrast-enhanced abdominal computed tomography (CT) revealed a 6-cm mass along the gastric antrum with apparent hepatic invasion and concurrent features of SBO. The gallbladder was not visualized. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) demonstrated a subepithelial tumor-like bulge with a small mucosal opening in the gastric antrum, raising suspicion of a fistulous tract. Interventions Emergency exploratory laparotomy identified two phytobezoars in the small bowel, which were treated by segmental resection and primary anastomosis. The gastric mass was found to be densely adherent to the liver, and bile leakage was encountered during dissection, prompting intraoperative hepatobiliary consultation. Outcomes Histopathological examination of the resected specimen confirmed GA with inflammatory granulation tissue at the gallbladder-gastric serosal interface, with no evidence of malignancy. The patient recovered uneventfully and was discharged 29 days postoperatively. Lessons This case highlights a novel and clinically significant diagnostic pitfall: GA-induced CGF can convincingly simulate an invasive gastric neoplasm on multimodal imaging and endoscopy. Recognition of biliary red flags, including non-visualization of the gallbladder on CT, a mucosal opening adjacent to a subepithelial-appearing lesion on EGD, and intramural cystic foci on imaging, is essential for accurate preoperative diagnosis.

title: Challenges in glaucoma diagnosis in small optic discs: An OCT-based analysis.
abstract: This study aimed to assess how optic disc (OD) size influences structural and functional tests in patients with glaucoma with small and normal-sized discs and to compare the sensitivities of these tests. The study comprised 182 eyes, including 109 eyes of 73 patients diagnosed with glaucoma and 73 eyes of 41 healthy subjects. Eyes were classified according to OD size as either small (<1.6 mm2) or normal (1.6-2.1 mm2). Optic nerve head parameters, peripapillary retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL) thickness, and macular ganglion cell analysis were assessed using Cirrus 4000 spectral-domain optical coherence tomography. The sensitivities of RNFL, macular ganglion cell-inner plexiform layer (GCIPL), and visual field parameters were evaluated using logistic receiver operating characteristic regression analysis. The mean ages of the patients and controls were 65.48 ± 7.94 years and 65.22 ± 6.55 years, respectively (P = .859). The mean disc diameter was 1.48 ± 0.11 mm in the small-disc group and 1.86 ± 0.16 mm in the normal-disc group. The mean deviation values were -5.52 ± 4.81 and -4.54 ± 3.73 in the small- and normal-disc groups, respectively (P = .268). Among patients with glaucoma and small ODs, GCIPL parameters (mean, minimum, superior, and inferior hemifield values) demonstrated greater sensitivity than RNFL parameters. In contrast, RNFL parameters (average, superior, inferior, and corresponding hemifield values) showed greater sensitivity than GCIPL parameters in patients with normal-sized ODs. Macular structural parameters demonstrated higher sensitivity for glaucoma diagnosis in patients with small ODs. However, a comprehensive assessment integrating both macular and peripapillary structural parameters may improve diagnostic accuracy by providing complementary information in these patients.

title: The role of total vaginal hysterectomy versus total abdominal hysterectomy in surgical management of uterine myomas: A retrospective single center cohort study.
abstract: Total vaginal hysterectomy (TVH) has been performed even for enlarged uterine myoma, but it is regarded as more inferior than total abdominal hysterectomy (TAH). The aim of this study was to compare the role of surgical choice in patients undergoing either TVH or TAH for uterine myoma. In this retrospective cohort study, 140 hysterectomies with bilateral adnexectomy were planned for postmenopausal women with uterine myoma between 2020 and 2024, in a tertiary center hospital. The diagnosis was established after clinical symptomatology and transvaginal ultrasound, with histopathological confirmation obtained postoperatively. The patients were divided into 2 groups: the TVH group (n = 70) and the TAH group (n = 70). Patient features such as age, uterine weight, body mass index (BMI), parity, operative time, intraoperative blood loss, hospital stay, medical history, surgical history, intra and postoperative complications, and adhesions were assessed. Mean age, uterine weight, BMI, and parity showed no significant difference between the groups. Instead, the TVH group was linked with significantly shorter operative time, lower intraoperative blood loss, and reduced hospital stay compared to the TAH group (P < .001). However, there were more medical and surgical histories in patients from the TAH group compared with the TVH group, including postoperative complications (11.44% vs 4.29%) and adhesions (32.86% vs 20%). In most cases, uterine hemisection, tactical myomectomy, or morcellation were used in order to reduce uterine size for the TVH group (78.57%). Our findings sustain that shorter operating time, lower intraoperative blood loss, and reduced hospital stay recommend TVH as a suitable choice in carefully selected postmenopausal women with enlarged uterine myoma.

title: Diagnosis of ankylosing spondylitis: A bibliometric review from 2008 to 2024.
abstract: Background The pathogenesis and pathological progression of ankylosing spondylitis (AS) remain unclear. Owing to the absence of a gold standard for diagnosing AS, diagnostic delays are frequently encountered in clinical practice, exacerbating the disease burden. In the past 16 years, several diagnostic studies on AS have been published. This study aimed to summarize the developmental trends and frontier hotspots in AS diagnosis through a bibliometric review. Methods Data were extracted from English publications on AS diagnosis from the Web of Science Core Collection (January 1, 2008-October 21, 2024). CiteSpace, VOSviewer, and the Biblioshiny R package were used to analyze the overview of the publication output, countries/regions, institutions, authors, sources, references, and keywords. Results A total of 1205 articles from 396 journals across 65 countries were included. The highest annual output occurred in 2021 (n = 111, 9.21%), whereas 2015 had the highest average number of citations (n = 5.1). Clinical Rheumatology (n = 76, 6.31%) was the most influential journal. China (n = 244, 20.25%), Berlin Institute of Health (n = 116, 9.63%), and Sieper J (n = 28, 2.32%) ranked first in terms of country, institution, and author productivity, respectively. The top 3 reference clusters were "diagnostic criteria," "therapeutics," and "recommendations." Burst detection identified 4 emerging post-2021 keywords: "children," "cells," "spondyloarthritis," and "expression." Conclusion AS diagnosis research has evolved through a growth phase (2008-2021), followed by a transitional or reorientation phase (2022-2024). Magnetic resonance imaging, Mendelian randomization, and biomarkers are current hotspots; Mendelian randomization serves as an etiological adjunct with the potential to inform biomarker discovery, though its findings do not yet constitute diagnostic tools. The apparent slowdown in recent years largely reflects evolving terminology (AS vs radiographic axial spondyloarthritis) and bibliometric time-lag bias rather than true intellectual stagnation, alongside fragmented pathophysiological insights and a lack of specific clinical features.

title: Androgen insensitivity syndrome: A case report.
abstract: Rationale 46, XY disorder of sex development (46, XY DSD) is relatively rare and frequently missed in clinical practice, necessitating early standardized diagnosis and treatment. Androgen insensitivity syndrome (AIS), a major subtype, should be considered in phenotypic females with suggestive clinical clues. Patient concerns A 29-year-old phenotypic female presented with primary amenorrhea and intermittent abdominal pain. Examination revealed normal breast development, sparse pubic hair, and female external genitalia. Pelvic ultrasonography and CT showed an absent uterus and ovaries, with bilateral inguinal masses. Diagnoses The case met the 3 diagnostic criteria for 46, XY DSD: 46,XY karyotype, testicular tissue, and feminized external genitalia. A diagnosis clinically consistent with complete AIS was further supported by the characteristic phenotype - female appearance, normal breast development, sparse pubic hair, and absent Müllerian structures. Other etiologies of undervirilization, including 5α-reductase deficiency and 17β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase deficiency, were considered. Genetic confirmation was unavailable, limiting subtype certainty. Interventions Following counseling, the patient underwent laparoscopic bilateral orchiectomy as prophylactic gonadectomy to reduce malignancy risk, together with inguinal hernia repair, followed by postoperative hormone replacement therapy. Postoperative histopathology confirmed testicular tissue with Leydig cell hyperplasia, absent spermatogenic cells, and no malignancy. Outcomes Abdominal pain resolved postoperatively, with improved psychological well-being and adaptation to the diagnosis under ongoing endocrine and psychological support. Lessons 46, XY DSD is underdiagnosed due to phenotypic variability, reliance on specialized tests, and social biases. AIS should be considered in the differential diagnosis of phenotypic females presenting with primary amenorrhea, developed secondary sexual characteristics, and an absent uterus on ultrasound. However, definitive subtyping requires AR gene sequencing, which was not available in this case. Early diagnosis requires careful assessment of newborn external genitalia, with specialist evaluation prompted by any atypical findings, and hormonal and genetic testing in adolescents with abnormal development. Multidisciplinary care - involving gynecologists, endocrinologists, surgeons, geneticists, and mental-health professionals - is essential for comprehensive management, including psychological support, hormone therapy, and timely prophylactic gonadectomy. Establishing specialized multidisciplinary centers for DSD is also recommended.

title: Pulmonary cryptococcosis mimicking metastatic progression despite systemic disease stability in advanced colon cancer: A case report and literature review.
abstract: Rationale In patients with advanced cancer, newly detected pulmonary nodules are often interpreted as metastatic progression. The distinctive feature of this case was the appearance of multiple new lung nodules during otherwise controlled systemic disease: the primary colonic lesion and hepatic metastases remained stable while tumor marker levels declined. This radiologic-clinical discordance prompted reconsideration of metastatic progression and broadened the differential diagnosis. Patient concerns A patient with advanced colon cancer, who was undergoing systemic chemotherapy and had otherwise stable disease, was found to have developed new pulmonary nodules on routine surveillance imaging. The patient was entirely asymptomatic from a respiratory standpoint. The primary clinical concern was the discordance between the radiologically suspicious findings and the patient's overall stable clinical condition. Diagnoses The initial radiologic impression favored pulmonary metastases. However, multidisciplinary review recognized the discordance between the new lung lesions and the otherwise stable systemic disease and raised concern for an opportunistic infection. Serum (1,3)-β-D-glucan and qualitative cryptococcal capsular polysaccharide antigen tests were positive, supporting a diagnosis of pulmonary cryptococcosis. Interventions After cerebrospinal fluid evaluation excluded central nervous system involvement, fluconazole 400 mg once daily was initiated. The anticancer strategy was not escalated on the basis of the pulmonary findings alone. Outcomes Follow-up chest computed tomography demonstrated marked regression of the pulmonary nodules. Lessons When new pulmonary lesions arise despite stability or response at established tumor sites, apparent radiologic progression should not automatically be equated with oncologic progression. Integrating the longitudinal treatment response, tumor marker trends, clinical symptoms, imaging features, and targeted infectious testing can prevent unnecessary changes in cancer therapy and may avoid invasive procedures when a sufficiently supported alternative diagnosis is available.

title: Biodegradable pins fixation for lateral condylar fracture of the humerus in children: A retrospective study of biodegradable pin fixation combined with versus without absorbable tension band wiring.
abstract: Biodegradable pins are increasingly used in the treatment of lateral condylar fractures of the humerus (LCFH) in children, but the strength of the biodegradable pin is weaker than that of K-wire. However, to enhance the stability of LCFH fixed by biodegradable pins, absorbable tension band wiring is often combined with the application, yet high-quality comparative evidence verifying the clinical value of this auxiliary reinforcement remains lacking. This study aimed to compare and analyze whether auxiliary absorbable tension band wiring has clinical significance for Weiss type III LCFH and to clarify whether additional tension band fixation is clinically necessary in reducing postoperative complications and improving fracture stability. This study enrolled 96 children with Weiss type III LCFH admitted between January 2017 and September 2019. The patients were divided into 2 groups: A (fixed by 3 biodegradable pins alone, n = 45) and B (fixed by 3 biodegradable pins and combined with the application of absorbable figure-of-eight tension band wiring, n = 51). Preoperative, intraoperative, and postoperative indicators, including age, sex, operation time, intraoperative blood loss, fracture healing time, elbow functional recovery time, and postoperative complications, were compared between the 2 groups. Postoperative elbow function was assessed by using the Flynn grading system. All radiographic measurements and functional evaluations were performed by 2 calibrated orthopedic surgeons with excellent inter-rater reliability. Sample size calculations were performed before data collection to guarantee statistical validity. There were no significant differences in age, sex, injured side, preoperative fracture displacement, operation duration, intraoperative blood loss, fracture healing time, elbow functional recovery time, or Flynn functional grading (all P > .05). Complete fracture union was observed in all patients, and no adverse complications, such as wound infection, bone nonunion, osteonecrosis, or elbow deformity, occurred in either group. Absorbable tension band wiring reinforcement is not required after biodegradable pin fixation in the treatment of LCFH in children.

title: Suspected allergic bronchopulmonary candidiasis in a patient with concurrent multidrug-resistant bacterial pneumonia: A case report.
abstract: Rationale Allergic bronchopulmonary candidiasis (ABPC) is a rare pulmonary hypersensitivity disorder; diagnosis is difficult because Candida albicans is usually a respiratory commensal. Patient concerns A 70-year-old man with hypertension and prior cerebral infarction was admitted for sudden right limb weakness (6.5 hours) and diagnosed with hemorrhagic cerebral infarction in the intensive care unit. Diagnoses Persistent fever and pulmonary infiltrates developed despite broad-spectrum antibiotics. Total immunoglobulin E (IgE) was 2181 IU/mL; sputum grew C albicans + carbapenem-resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa; bronchoalveolar lavage fluid metagenomic next-generation sequencing detected C albicans, P aeruginosa, Klebsiella pneumoniae, EBV, and HSV-1. ABPC was suspected alongside multidrug-resistant bacterial pneumonia. Interventions Ceftazidime-avibactam (2.5 g q8h) + nebulized polymyxin B (0.5 M IU q12h); oral voriconazole (400 mg q12h loading, then 200 mg q12h); IV methylprednisolone 40 mg/d. Outcomes Clinical improvement on combined therapy; respiratory stabilization within 2 weeks; intensive care unit transfer out. Follow-up chest computed tomography showed resolution of infiltrates; total IgE fell from 2181 to 995 IU/mL (-54%). Discharged with hemorrhagic cerebral infarction, hypertension, carbapenem-resistant Pseudomonas pneumonia, K pneumoniae co-infection, and ABPM. Lessons Persistent infiltrates with high IgE and Candida isolation should suggest ABPM, not intensified antibiotics. ABPC can occur in older patients without asthma. Early corticosteroids plus antifungals yield rapid improvement. Metagenomic next-generation sequencing complements conventional testing but cannot confirm ABPC alone.

title: Primary pulmonary mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue lymphoma presenting as a right hilar mass: A case report.
abstract: Rationale Primary pulmonary lymphoma (PPL) is an extremely rare malignant lung tumor that is frequently misdiagnosed as pneumonia or lung cancer due to its atypical radiological and clinical presentation. The rationale of this report is to elucidate the diagnostic value of combining computed tomography (CT) and 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography/computed tomography (18F-FDG PET/CT) in evaluating a rare presentation of PPL. Patient concerns A 44-year-old male was admitted after an incidental lung lesion was discovered during routine screening. He was completely asymptomatic, lacking respiratory or systemic "B symptoms." Diagnoses A baseline chest CT identified a 3.9 × 3.5 cm soft-tissue mass in the right hilar region that compressed the right upper lobe bronchus, leading to secondary post-obstructive consolidation that lacked the characteristic air bronchogram sign. The CT also revealed an incidental 2.6 × 2.6 cm anterior mediastinal nodule. Subsequent whole-body 18F-FDG PET/CT demonstrated intense tracer uptake in the right hilar mass with a maximum standardized uptake value of 7.1 and mild-to-moderate uptake in an adjacent regional lymph node (maximum standardized uptake value of 3.2). The scan showed completely absent uptake in the anterior mediastinal nodule and the post-obstructive consolidation, arguing against metabolically active malignancy in those areas. Histopathological and immunohistochemical analysis from a bronchoscopic transbronchial lung biopsy confirmed primary pulmonary mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue lymphoma. Interventions The patient underwent localized radiotherapy targeting the right hilar mass and the FDG-avid regional hilar/posterior mediastinal lymph node. A total dose of 66 Gy was delivered in 18 fractions over the course of 3 weeks. Outcomes At the 2-month post-discharge follow-up, a repeat chest CT revealed a marked reduction in the size of both the hilar lesion and the regional lymph nodes. The patient remained completely asymptomatic, and his laboratory parameters normalized. Lessons Differentiating PPL from central lung cancer and coexisting benign mediastinal abnormalities presents a significant clinical challenge, particularly when atypical radiological features mimic aggressive carcinomas. Whole-body 18F-FDG PET/CT serves as an invaluable, noninvasive modality for metabolic characterization, accurate loco-regional staging, and preventing clinical overstaging by effectively differentiating metabolically active lymphoma from concurrent benign lesions.

title: Excellent response to high-dose Riboflavin in Brown-Vialetto-Van Laere syndrome: A case report.
abstract: Rationale Brown-Vialetto-Van Laere syndrome, currently recognized within the spectrum of riboflavin transporter deficiency type 3 (RTD3), is a rare inherited neurometabolic disorder associated with pathogenic variants in SLC52A3. It typically presents with progressive sensorineural hearing loss, pontobulbar dysfunction, peripheral neuropathy, and respiratory involvement. Diagnosis may be delayed because routine metabolic and neuromuscular investigations can be unrevealing despite a characteristic clinical phenotype. Patient concerns A young Asian man presented with several years of progressive bilateral hearing loss followed by worsening dysphagia to solids and liquids, symmetrical limb weakness, muscle wasting, and acute-on-chronic dyspnea. Two siblings had previously died at a young age after developing a similar sequence of hearing impairment, dysphagia, limb weakness, and unexplained respiratory failure. Diagnoses Neurological examination showed tongue atrophy with fasciculations, thenar wasting, bifacial weakness, mild ptosis, diminished gag reflex, and symmetrical limb weakness. Audiometry confirmed profound bilateral sensorineural hearing loss. Nerve conduction studies demonstrated predominantly motor axonal neuropathy, while electromyography showed chronic and active denervation. Repetitive nerve stimulation, cerebrospinal fluid analysis, magnetic resonance imaging, creatine kinase levels, and metabolic investigations were unrevealing. Targeted genetic testing detected pathogenic SLC52A3 variants, confirming RTD3/ Brown-Vialetto-Van Laere syndrome. Interventions High-dose oral riboflavin was initiated empirically at 40 mg/kg/day in 3 divided doses before genetic confirmation because of progressive respiratory compromise and strong clinical suspicion. Supportive management included nutritional support and nocturnal noninvasive ventilation with bilevel positive airway pressure. Outcomes The patient showed marked improvement after riboflavin initiation. Respiratory effort improved within several days, and forced vital capacity increased from 35% to 50% of predicted within 1 week. Limb strength improved, and by 8 weeks the patient had gained 3 kg with stabilization of dysphagia and improved oral intake. At 6 months, neurological status remained stable without further electrophysiological progression. Riboflavin was well tolerated. Lessons RTD3 should be considered in young patients with progressive sensorineural hearing loss associated with bulbar dysfunction, motor neuropathy, or respiratory weakness, particularly when family history is suggestive. Recognition of the characteristic phenotype, targeted genetic testing, and prompt initiation of high-dose riboflavin may substantially alter the clinical course of this potentially treatable disorder.

title: Concordance of p16 status between US-guided core needle biopsy and surgical specimens in oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma: A diagnostic accuracy study.
abstract: With the increasing prevalence of human papillomavirus (HPV)-driven oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma (OPSCC), there is a need for efficient, minimally invasive methods to evaluate p16 status. This study aimed to assess the concordance of p16 status between ultrasound (US)-guided core needle biopsy (CNB) of cervical lymph nodes and surgical specimens, and to describe the numbers of CNB and surgical sessions required to establish the histopathologic diagnosis. This retrospective study included 39 patients diagnosed with OPSCC or head and neck squamous cell carcinoma of unknown primary (SCCUP) at a single tertiary hospital between March 2019 and March 2024. All included patients underwent US-guided CNB of cervical lymph nodes and a surgical procedure (biopsy or resection), and had evaluable p16 immunohistochemistry (IHC) results on both specimen types. The concordance rate for p16 status between US-guided CNB and surgical specimens was 100.0% (39/39; 95% CI, 91.0-100.0%; 35 p16-positive and 4 p16-negative cases). Sensitivity was 100.0% (35/35; 95% CI, 90.0-100.0%) and specificity was 100.0% (4/4; 95% CI, 39.8-100.0%). In all 39 included patients, a diagnosis of metastatic squamous cell carcinoma and an evaluable p16 result were obtained at the first CNB session. Among the 35 patients with OPSCC, 10 (28.6%) required more than 1 surgical session at the primary tumor site. No immediate complications were observed following US-guided CNB. In this cohort, US-guided CNB of cervical lymph nodes showed complete observed concordance with surgical specimens for p16 status, and a diagnosis with an evaluable p16 result was obtained at the first CNB session in all patients. Prospective, multicenter validation including more p16-negative cases is required before wider adoption.

title: Outcomes of sequential keratoplasty for bilateral gelatinous drop-like corneal dystrophy: A case report.
abstract: Rationale Gelatinous drop-like corneal dystrophy (GDLD) is a rare autosomal recessive disorder characterized by subepithelial amyloid deposition, progressive corneal opacification, and recurrent erosions. GDLD may present during the first decade of life and interfere with visual development. It may recur after keratoplasty, complicating surgical management. Patient concerns A 21-year-old woman of Yemeni ancestry, living in a remote area with limited access to corneal transplantation, presented with progressive left eye visual decline and foreign body sensation since early childhood. She had long-standing bilateral visual impairment and a positive family history. Her first surgery was right eye penetrating keratoplasty (PK), performed elsewhere approximately 1 year earlier for an undiagnosed opacity. Diagnoses Examination revealed nystagmus, a clear right graft with yellowish recipient deposits, and dense limbus-to-limbus left corneal opacification with stromal haze, mulberry-like deposits, and neovascularization. Uncorrected visual acuity (VA) was 20/200 in the right eye and counting fingers in the left. Best spectacle-corrected VA was 20/100 in the right eye, while reliable refraction could not be obtained in the left. Histopathology demonstrated Congo red-positive subepithelial amyloid deposits with birefringence under polarized light, confirming GDLD. Genetic testing for tumor-associated calcium signal transducer 2 was not performed. Interventions The left eye underwent superficial keratectomy and attempted lamellar dissection assisted by intraoperative optical coherence tomography; dense deep stromal opacity necessitated conversion to full-thickness PK. Outcomes Both grafts remained clear without rejection during follow-up. Minimal focal subepithelial haze in a temporal area of the left donor graft was noted at the 2 most recent visits, remained stationary between them, and was clinically insignificant. At final follow-up, approximately 2 years after right eye PK and 10 months after left eye PK, best spectacle-corrected VA was 20/100 in the right eye and 20/80 - 1 in the left. Intraocular pressure was normal, and posterior pole examinations were unremarkable. Lessons Advanced bilateral GDLD poses clinical and surgical challenges. PK may restore corneal clarity and provide meaningful visual rehabilitation, although recovery may remain incomplete after early-onset visual impairment and delayed treatment. Long-term monitoring is essential because recurrence and repeat intervention may be required. Early recognition, timely referral, and individualized management matter where donor corneal tissue access is limited.

title: Bibliometric analysis and visualization of adenomyosis: From 1980-2024.
abstract: Objectives This bibliometric analysis systematically evaluated the research landscape, emerging trends, and key focus areas in adenomyosis to guide future research directions. Design Performance analysis combined with scientific mapping of global adenomyosis research literature. Data sources Web of Science Core Collection (1980-2024). Data extraction and synthesis Articles were manually screened. Bibliometrix (R 4.3.0), VOSviewer, and CiteSpace analyzed productivity, collaboration, citation patterns, and research trends. Derived data and analysis scripts are deposited in the Open Science Framework (OSF) under a citable DOI. Results Among 3100 included publications, China led output (752, 24.26%, full-counted), followed by the United States (414, 13.35%), Japan (350, 11.29%), Italy (215, 6.94%), and South Korea (128, 4.13%). In the 2 adenomyosis-specific corpora, however, the United States ranked first. The US had the highest citations and international collaboration, though international co-authorship among top-producing countries remained low (16.14%). Leading institutions were Fudan University (89), Shandong University (52), and University of Tokyo (49). Top journals by volume: Fertility and Sterility, Human Reproduction, and Journal of Minimally Invasive Gynecology. Research focus shifted from hysterectomy and uterine artery embolization toward high-intensity focused ultrasound (HIFU), and from endothelial nitric oxide synthase/induced adenomyosis toward ectopic endometrium. Eight keyword clusters emerged; the 4 largest (#0 EMT, #1 HIFU, #2 endometrial cancer, #3 pregnancy outcomes) form the present focus. Performance analysis combined with scientific mapping of global adenomyosis research literature.

Web of Science Core Collection (1980-2024).

title: Staged bilateral reverse sural artery flap reconstruction for severe frostbite of both feet in a patient with schizophrenia: A case report.
abstract: Rationale Bilateral, weight-bearing heel defects after frostbite are difficult to reconstruct, and outcomes depend heavily on postoperative off-loading and patient cooperation. We report a limb-salvage strategy for severe bilateral foot frostbite that occurred during acute psychosis in a patient diagnosed with schizophrenia. Patient concerns A 25-year-old man developed acute psychotic symptoms and walked barefoot in subzero conditions for about 12 hours, resulting in deep frostbite of both heels and multiple toes. During admission he had poor insight and repeatedly attempted weight bearing despite instructions. Diagnoses MRI/CT showed necrosis of the right first to third toes and bilateral posterior heel soft-tissue necrosis with preserved deep heel structures, supporting flap-based salvage rather than major amputation. Schizophrenia was diagnosed and treated concurrently. Interventions Reconstruction was staged. The right first to third toes were amputated, the right heel was debrided, and coverage was achieved with a reverse sural artery flap (RSAF). Three weeks later, the left great toe underwent debridement with split-thickness skin grafting, and the left heel defect was reconstructed with an RSAF. Strict positioning/off-loading and close multidisciplinary inpatient supervision were used to protect both flaps while psychiatric symptoms were stabilized. Outcomes At the last documented follow-up, 2 weeks after discharge - corresponding to 5 weeks after the left-sided reconstruction and approximately 8 weeks after the right-sided reconstruction - both flaps remained viable, with no total flap loss or flap-related reoperation, and small residual superficial wounds remained. No subsequent clinical follow-up was available. Lessons In frostbite patients with severe mental illness, reconstructive choice should balance technical "ideal" options against real-world feasibility. In this patient, staged regional flap reconstruction provided short-term wound coverage while accommodating psychiatric stabilization and limited adherence; however, long-term durability could not be assessed.

title: Multidimensional patterns of malocclusion in treatment-seeking Turkish orthodontic patients: A retrospective cross-sectional study.
abstract: Malocclusion is a common craniofacial disorder with significant functional and aesthetic implications. Although sagittal, vertical, and transverse discrepancies frequently coexist, most prevalence studies evaluate these traits separately. This study aimed to analyze the prevalence and multidimensional interactions of sagittal, vertical, and transverse malocclusions in a large Turkish treatment-seeking orthodontic cohort using artificial intelligence-assisted overbite measurements for standardized vertical assessment. A retrospective cross-sectional analysis was performed on standardized intraoral photographs and cephalometric radiographs of 2624 treatment-seeking orthodontic patients (1125 males and 1499 females) treated at a tertiary referral university clinic between 2007 and 2020. Sagittal malocclusions were classified according to Angle's classification (class I, II, and III). Transverse relationships were defined by the presence or absence of posterior crossbite, while vertical subgroups were established using artificial intelligence-assisted overbite measurements for standardized vertical assessment. Chi-square tests with Bonferroni-adjusted pairwise comparisons and multinomial logistic regression were performed. Class II malocclusion was the most prevalent sagittal malocclusion (49.1%), followed by class I (33.0%) and class III (17.9%). Normal transverse relationships predominated in class I (54.3%) and class II (66.9%), whereas more than half of class III individuals exhibited posterior crossbite (57.9%). In class I and II, posterior crossbite was seen more frequently in open bite cases and was least common in deep bite cases. In class III, posterior crossbite prevalence remained high across all vertical subgroups, regardless of overbite pattern. Multinomial logistic regression showed that deep bite had the strongest independent association with class II malocclusion, whereas bilateral posterior crossbite had the strongest independent association with class III malocclusion. The prevalence of orthodontic malocclusions should be evaluated using a multidimensional approach that considers the coexistence of sagittal, vertical, and transverse discrepancies rather than assessing each occlusal dimension independently. The strong association between class III malocclusion and posterior crossbite, together with the vertical-transverse interactions observed in class I and II, highlights the importance of comprehensive multidimensional orthodontic assessment and individualized treatment planning. Recognizing these multidimensional patterns may facilitate comprehensive clinical assessment and guide future epidemiological research.

title: Risk factors for perioperative venous thromboembolism in patients undergoing colorectal cancer surgery: A single-center retrospective study.
abstract: Venous thromboembolism (VTE), including deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism, is a serious perioperative complication after colorectal cancer surgery. Although guidelines recommend prophylaxis, bleeding risks complicate decision-making, and evidence regarding Japanese patients remains limited. Therefore, this study aimed to identify perioperative risk factors associated with VTE in colorectal cancer surgery to inform effective risk stratification and targeted prevention strategies. A retrospective analysis of 397 patients who underwent elective colorectal cancer resection at a single institution between June 2014 and May 2024 was conducted. Preoperative and postoperative D-dimer levels were measured, and lower extremity venous ultrasonography was performed when indicated. When deep vein thrombosis was detected by venous ultrasonography, contrast-enhanced computed tomography was subsequently performed to evaluate the presence of pulmonary embolism. Univariate analyses were used to determine factors significantly associated with VTE, and a P-value < .05 was considered statistically significant. Preoperative VTE was observed in nine of 397 patients (2.3%), and postoperative VTE was observed in nine of 388 patients (2.3%). The univariate analysis suggested that age ≥75 years, female gender, albumin levels < 3.5 g/dL, and hemoglobin levels < 10 g/dL were significantly associated with preoperative VTE, while operative time ≥ 240 minutes and intraoperative blood loss ≥ 50 mL were significantly associated with postoperative VTE. Advanced age, female gender, hypoalbuminemia, anemia, prolonged operative time, and increased intraoperative blood loss were significantly associated with perioperative VTE in univariate analysis. Effective perioperative risk stratification and targeted surveillance may contribute to the early detection and prevention of VTE in Japanese patients undergoing colorectal cancer surgery.

title: Peritoneal dialysis catheter dysfunction: when can the catheter be rescued?
abstract: Purpose of review Peritoneal dialysis (PD) catheter dysfunction is frequently treated as a generic access failure, although the appropriate response depends on the underlying mechanism. This review summarizes a practical, mechanism-directed approach to reversible medical causes, image-guided salvage, surgical revision, and catheter replacement. Recent findings Recent guidelines and reviews support early exclusion of infection and acute abdominal pathology, deliberate treatment of constipation and fibrin, and early abdominal radiography when flow is impaired. Catheterography and fluoroscopic manipulation can restore selected migrated or partially obstructed catheters. Still, immediate technical success does not ensure durable function when omental wrap, adhesions, fixed kinking, or unfavorable catheter geometry is present. Observational series also support same-session removal and reinsertion for noninfectious mechanical failure and for narrowly selected infection-related indications. Laparoscopic revision remains the definitive treatment for structural abnormalities. Summary A successful PD access program requires a written rescue pathway that quickly transitions from reversible causes to mechanism-specific interventions. The meaningful outcome is not radiographic catheter position alone, but rapid return to the prescribed PD regimen while minimizing temporary hemodialysis exposure, repeated emergency visits, and avoidable technique failure.

title: Relationship between extent of jeopardized myocardium derived from myocardial viability study to post-myocardial infarction outcome.
abstract: Objective This study aimed to assess the relationship between the extent of jeopardized myocardium, quantified using cardiac viability imaging, and clinical outcomes in patients after myocardial infarction. By utilizing rest myocardial perfusion imaging (MPI) and cardiac 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose PET/computed tomography (18F-FDG PET/CT) analyzed with Emory Cardiac Toolbox software (ECTb), the study aimed to determine how quantitative viability parameters correlate with left ventricular functional recovery and post-myocardial infarction outcomes, and to assess their utility in guiding clinical decision-making. Methods This prospective study included 85 patients who underwent 2-day rest MPI followed by cardiac FDG-PET/CT imaging. Quantitative parameters, including the percentage of jeopardized myocardium, comprising viable, scarred, and total jeopardized myocardial segments, along with left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) were obtained using the ECTb platform (version 4.2). The relationship between these quantitative PET parameters and functional myocardial recovery, defined as improvement in ≥5% LVEF as assessed by two-dimensional echocardiography, was evaluated using receiver operating characteristic curve analysis. Follow-up was conducted over a period of 3 months, 6 months, and 1 year to assess the association between baseline quantitative imaging parameters and the occurrence of adverse cardiac events. Results The analysis demonstrated that the extent of viable myocardium was a strong predictor of functional recovery (area under the curve, 0.762; P < 0.001), with a cutoff of approximately 17% yielding 76.7% sensitivity, 68.8% specificity, and 71.8% accuracy. Major adverse cardiac events (MACE) occurred in 16% of patients. There was no significant association with imaging parameters, except a nonsignificant trend for scar burden in medically managed patients. Patients undergoing surgical intervention had a significantly greater extent of jeopardized myocardium, underscoring the role of viability imaging in therapeutic decision-making. Conclusion The extent of viable myocardium identified through imaging was strongly correlated with functional recovery, as reflected by improvements in cardiac function on follow-up echocardiography. Although no significant relationship with MACE was seen in the overall cohort, the higher burden of jeopardized myocardium in surgically treated patients underscores the value of viability imaging in guiding revascularization decisions, supporting FDG-PET/CT as a useful tool for post-myocardial infarction risk stratification and management.

title: The impact and value of [18F]-FDG PET-CT on management of patients with cervical cancer with service evaluation audited against national evidence-based PET-CT guidelines.
abstract: Purpose First, to assess the diagnostic value of fluorine-18-fluorodeoxyglucose PET-computed tomography ([18F]-FDG PET-CT) compared with conventional MRI and/or CT. Second, to audit the clinical indications for referring patients with cervical cancer for [18F]-FDG PET-CT against the 2022 guidelines published by the Royal College of Radiologists and the Royal College of Physicians. Finally, to evaluate the impact of [18F]-FDG PET-CT on management plans. Methods A retrospective cohort study of 49 patients with histologically proven cervical cancer across the Sussex Cancer Network underwent 59 [18F]-FDG PET-CT between 1 November 2020 and 31 October 2022. Scans were compared with the most recent CT and MRI scan conducted within 4 months of the [18F]-FDG PET-CT. Scan indications were categorized as either 'in accordance' or 'outside' the guidelines. Those in accordance fell into one of four groups: staging, response assessment, suspected recurrence, or staging when considering exenterative surgery. A questionnaire investigating the impact of the [18F]-FDG PET-CT on the management plan of each patient was answered by one clinical oncology consultant. Results [18F]-FDG PET-CT identified new metastatic sites in 16/59 (27.1%) scans. The remaining scans were concordant with the CT and MRI. The majority, 57/59 (96.6%), of the scans were performed in accordance with the guidelines. The management plan was changed by 5/59 scans (8.4%), confirmed by 48/59 (81.4%) and was not impacted with 6/59 (10.2%) scans. Conclusion [18F]-FDG PET-CT is superior to conventional imaging and enhances the management plan. Future cohort studies with larger patient numbers involving multicentric studies are needed to fully assess its impact on cervical cancer management and prognosis.

title: Artificial intelligence in personalized internal dosimetry for radiopharmaceutical therapy: a narrative mini-review.
abstract: Personalized internal radiation dosimetry supports individualized radiopharmaceutical therapy but remains difficult to implement because workflows require repeated quantitative imaging, segmentation, registration, kinetic modeling, and absorbed-dose calculation. This mini-review summarizes current evidence on artificial intelligence across the personalized dosimetry workflow and considers clinical readiness. A narrative PubMed search was completed in early 2026 and covered peer-reviewed studies published from 2015 to early 2026. Studies addressing artificial intelligence, machine learning, or deep learning in quantitative image reconstruction, segmentation, registration, time-activity curve estimation, absorbed-dose calculation, or clinical decision support were considered. Studies reporting quantitative performance or validation results were prioritized. Deep learning reduced yttrium-90 single-photon emission computed tomography reconstruction error from 149.5% ± 31.2% to 9.2% ± 1.7%; lesion dose-rate error was 8.6% ± 5.7% in virtual-patient testing. Learning-based registration reduced computation time from about 50 s to under 6 s. Single-time-point approaches can simplify imaging, and recent machine learning work has explored prediction of organ effective half-life. Automated segmentation methods show improving reproducibility, whereas evidence for artificial intelligence-based clinical decision support remains mainly retrospective and single-center. Artificial intelligence applications in reconstruction and segmentation appear closer to clinical readiness, while decision-support applications still require prospective, multicenter validation.

title: Preoperative 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose PET/computed tomography maximum standardized uptake value is independently associated with overall survival in surgically resected undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma.
abstract: Background Undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma (UPS) is the most common adult soft tissue sarcoma subtype, with heterogeneous survival despite optimal surgery. We evaluated whether the preoperative maximum standardized uptake value (SUVmax) on 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose PET/computed tomography (18F-FDG PET/CT) is independently associated with overall survival (OS) in surgically resected UPS. Methods This retrospective cohort study included 79 patients with localized UPS who underwent curative resection between 2015 and 2023. Preoperative SUVmax, tumor grade (French Federation of Cancer Centers Sarcoma Group), tumor size, and Ki-67 index were assessed. Cox proportional hazards regression was used to identify independent prognostic factors for OS. Results The median age was 59 (range: 18-92) years; 53.2% of patients were male, and 59.5% of tumors were high grade. The median tumor size, Ki-67 index, and SUVmax were 60 mm, 60%, and 10, respectively. At a median follow-up of 58.9 months, median OS was not reached. In univariable analysis, tumor size (P = 0.007), Ki-67 (P = 0.001), SUVmax [hazard ratio: 1.08 per unit, 95% confidence interval (CI): 1.04-1.10, P = 0.001], and high grade (P = 0.003) were associated with worse OS. In multivariable analysis, only SUVmax remained independently associated with OS (adjusted hazard ratio: 1.06 per unit, 95% CI: 1.02-1.10, P = 0.002), whereas grade, size, and Ki-67 did not retain significance. Conclusion Preoperative 18F-FDG PET/CT SUVmax is independently associated with OS in surgically resected UPS and provides prognostic information beyond conventional clinicopathological parameters.

In multivariable analysis, only SUVmax remained independently associated with OS (adjusted hazard ratio: 1.06 per unit, 95% CI: 1.02-1.10, P = 0.002), whereas grade, size, and Ki-67 did not retain significance.

Conclusion

Preoperative 18F-FDG PET/CT SUVmax is independently associated with OS in surgically resected UPS and provides prognostic information beyond conventional clinicopathological parameters.

title: Diagnostic accuracy of carbonic anhydrase IX-targeted PET/CT for detection of clear cell renal cell carcinoma in patients with renal masses: a systematic review and meta-analysis of diagnostic test accuracy studies.
abstract: The preoperative differentiation of clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC) from other renal masses remains challenging. Carbonic anhydrase IX (CAIX) is a highly specific target for noninvasive ccRCC imaging. We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis to determine the diagnostic accuracy of CAIX-targeted PET/computed tomography (CT) for differentiating ccRCC from non-ccRCC renal masses. A comprehensive search of PubMed, Embase, Scopus, and Registers (up to 30 September 2025) was supplemented by a bibliographic review. Studies evaluating CAIX-PET/CT against histopathologically were included. Of 528 records, five studies (n = 544 patients) were included. Pooled sensitivity and specificity were synthesized using a univariate fixed-effects model; predictive values, likelihood ratios, and diagnostic odds ratio were also calculated. For the detection of histopathologically confirmed ccRCC (vs. non-ccRCC renal masses), the pooled sensitivity was 85.5% [95% confidence interval (CI): 81.6-88.7] and specificity of 86.5 (95% CI: 80.4-90.9). The hierarchical summary receiver operating characteristic model yielded an area under the curve of 0.894. Exploratory subgroup analysis suggested a potential difference in diagnostic performance between the tracer subtypes. This review provides low-certainty evidence that CAIX-targeted PET/CT is a highly accurate, noninvasive tool for differentiating ccRCC from non-ccRCC renal masses in presurgical populations. Clinically, its high positive predictive value (94.6%) strongly 'rules in' disease, while its modest negative predictive value (~69%) limits its ability to 'rule out' malignancy. Further studies are warranted to validate these findings in broader clinical cohorts and for small-molecule agents.

title: Radiomics analysis of dynamic carbon-11 methionine PET/computed tomography for differentiating benign and malignant musculoskeletal lesions: a preliminary clinical assessment.
abstract: Objective To evaluate the diagnostic performance of radiomics features and maximum standardized uptake value (SUVmax) extracted from dynamic carbon-11 methionine (C-11 MET) PET/computed tomography (PET/CT) in differentiating malignant from benign musculoskeletal lesions (MSLs) and compare their performance with apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) values from magnetic resonance (MR) images. Methods This retrospective study included 15 patients (malignant: seven and benign: eight) with MSLs who underwent dynamic C-11 MET PET scans [5-15 (phase 1), 15-25 (phase 2), and 25-35 (phase 3) min postinjection of C-11 MET] and conventional acquisition (35 min postinjection). For semiquantitative analysis of MET uptake, we used SUVmax. For radiomics analysis, 109 features were extracted from the volume of interest for the entire target tumor in each dynamic phase. ADC values were measured from MR images. Diagnostic capacities were analyzed using the Mann-Whitney U test and receiver operating characteristic curve analyses. Results SUVmax for each dynamic phase and conventional acquisition was significantly higher in the malignant group than in the benign group (P < 0.05). In radiomics analysis, 70, 69, and 69 features in phases 1, 2, and 3, respectively, were significantly different between malignant and benign groups [P < 0.05; area under the ROC curves (AUCs) ≥ 0.821]. DeLong's test showed no significant difference in AUCs between SUVmax and any radiomics feature in each dynamic phase. ADC values did not differ significantly between malignant and benign groups. Conclusion Dynamic C-11 MET PET/CT has potential for differentiating malignant from benign MSLs and supports the utility of radiomics analyses and SUVmax.

title: 18F-FDG PET/MRI-based liver and bone marrow organomics combined with systemic inflammatory response for predicting pathological complete response after neoadjuvant therapy in breast cancer.
abstract: Objective To evaluate the role of liver and bone marrow organomics features derived from staging 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose (18F-FDG) PET/MRI in predicting pathological complete response (pCR) in breast cancer patients who underwent surgery after neoadjuvant therapy. Methods In this retrospective study, breast cancer patients who underwent pretreatment staging with 18F-FDG PET/MRI, received neoadjuvant therapy, and subsequently underwent surgery were included. Clinicopathological characteristics and systemic inflammatory markers were recorded. Organomics features were extracted from the liver and L4 vertebra bone marrow regions on 18F-FDG PET images using LIFEx software. Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator regression was applied for radiomics feature selection, and a radiomics score (Radscore) was generated. Logistic regression analyses were performed to identify predictors of pCR. The diagnostic performances of the Radscore, Clinical, and Clinical-Radscore Combined models were evaluated using receiver operating characteristic analysis. Results A total of 87 breast cancer patients were included, and pCR was observed in 33 patients (37.9%). In multivariable analysis, progesterone receptor status, human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 status, primary tumor size, and Radscore were identified as independent predictors of pCR. The Radscore yielded an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.722 [95% confidence interval (CI) = 0.625-0.819], whereas the Clinical and Clinical-Radscore Combined models achieved AUCs of 0.850 (95% CI = 0.765-0.934) and 0.904 (95% CI = 0.843-0.965), respectively. The Clinical-Radscore Combined Model demonstrated higher diagnostic performance than both the other models. Conclusion Liver and bone marrow organomics features derived from staging 18F-FDG PET/MRI may provide valuable information for predicting pCR in breast cancer patients undergoing neoadjuvant therapy.

title: Sleeve fractures of the patella: current concepts in diagnosis and surgical management.
abstract: Purpose of review Patella sleeve fractures are the most common patellar fracture in children yet remain frequently missed. Additionally, the options for their repair have grown. This review revisits how the injury is recognized and how the expanding range of fixation choices should be navigated. Recent findings Recent cohorts confirm that recognition rests on the examination rather than the radiograph, as the injury is frequently confused with Sinding-Larsen-Johansson syndrome. In sleeve fractures that are displaced or minimally displaced and in which the extensor mechanism is disrupted, operative treatment is recommended. Transosseous suture remains the most common technique, with suture anchors used for smaller fragments. No fixation method has proven superior, as no comparative trials have been conducted in pediatrics. Functional outcomes are good across treatment groups. However, patients with operative injuries return to sport more slowly, and hardware removal is common. Summary Patient outcomes depend less on the choice of fixation than on timely recognition. A high index of suspicion and knowledge of this type of injury help facilitate an accurate diagnosis. MRI-confirmed chondral injury and fracture-specific repair yield reliable outcomes. A delayed diagnosis remains the principal avoidable cause of treatment failure.

title: Prevalence and Clinical Significance of Abnormal Findings on Pre-Diagnostic Imaging in Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma.
abstract: Objectives Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is the third leading cause of cancer-related death. Although CT/MRI are used for initial evaluation, early imaging findings suggesting PDAC may be unappreciated, resulting in diagnostic delays. We aimed to determine the prevalence and types of pancreatic abnormalities on pre-diagnostic imaging in patients later diagnosed with PDAC. Methods We identified patients diagnosed with PDAC between 2022 and 2025 who had a pre-diagnostic abdominal CT/MRI performed 3-36 months before diagnostic imaging. These patients were compared with a non-PDAC cohort who underwent pancreas cancer screening but did not develop PDAC after 5 years of follow-up. The primary outcome was the prevalence and type of pancreatic abnormalities on pre-diagnostic scans. Results Among 733 PDAC patients, 151 (20.6%) had pre-diagnostic imaging (mean age 72.6 y, 53.6% F). At diagnosis, mean tumor size was 3.1 cm and 42.4% had metastatic disease. The mean (±SD) interval between pre-diagnostic and diagnostic scans was 15.9±9.5 months. Abnormal pancreaticobiliary findings were reported in 27.2% of pre-diagnostic scans. Pancreatic cyst prevalence was similar between pre-diagnostic and non-PDAC groups ( P =0.07). However, non-cyst pancreatic abnormalities were more frequent in PDAC pre-diagnostic scans ( P =0.04), including pancreatic duct dilation ( P =0.07) and pancreatic atrophy ( P =0.05). Conclusions Although >20% of PDAC patients had pre-diagnostic imaging, most pre-diagnostic scans reported no pancreatic abnormalities, despite eventual advanced disease at diagnosis. Subtle findings suggesting PDAC, such as duct dilation and pancreatic atrophy, were uncommon on pre-diagnostic scans but more frequent than in non-PDAC scans. These findings may represent early signs of PDAC and warrant closer surveillance.

title: Early Detection of Pancreatic Adenocarcinoma Using Triple-phase contrast-enhanced Computed Tomography: A Case-control Study.
abstract: Objectives To investigate the imaging findings of the triple-phase computed tomography (CT), which was performed prior to definitive diagnoses in patients with Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC). Methods The single-center, retrospective, case-control study included patients with PDAC who underwent triple-phase CT 3-36 months prior to definitive diagnosis (pre-diagnostic CT) between January 2007 and March 2018 in Teine Keijinkai hospital. Triple-phase CT in sex- and age-matched patients without PDAC appearance in a 4:1 ratio were selected as controls. Findings were detected from each of the five divided pancreatic sections on pre-diagnostic CT by radiologists' reviews, and were analyzed by comparison with CT at the definitive diagnosis (diagnostic CT) to investigate risk ratios. Results Pre-diagnostic CTs were investigated in 190 and 760 sections with 38 PDAC and 152 control patients. In the diagnostic CT, 50 PDAC-positive and 900 negative sections were detected, respectively. In pre-diagnostic CT review, some findings were shown in 17 (34.0%) and 18 (2.0%) sections among PDAC-positive and negative sections, respectively, and the total number of findings was 46 and 28 in PDAC-positive and negative sections, respectively. Finally, different attenuation of pancreatic parenchyma in each phase, MPD stenosis, and focal pancreatic parenchymal atrophy were significantly correlated with the risk of PDAC. Conclusions While some findings may already appear on the pre-diagnostic CT in one-third of the PDAC-positive sections, an accurate and detailed review in triple-phase CT is indispensable to detect early PDAC in clinical practice.

title: Urolithiasis in Pediatric Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia and Lymphoblastic Lymphoma (ALL/LLy): A Single-Center Case Series of Clinical, Metabolic, and Imaging Features.
abstract: Background Urolithiasis is an underrecognized complication in pediatric acute lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma (ALL/LLy), often associated with glucocorticoid therapy. Observations We report 4 cases of urolithiasis occurring at different diagnostic and treatment phases, 3 requiring intervention. Presenting symptoms included flank pain, hematuria, and urinary discomfort. In 1 case, renal abnormalities were incidentally identified on PET/CT performed for remission assessment. Conclusions Urolithiasis may occur across ALL/LLy diagnosis and treatment, particularly after glucocorticoid exposure and in patients with additional risk factors. Early recognition in patients with unexplained abdominal or urinary symptoms is essential to prevent complications.

title: Orbital volume measurement using direct measurement on 3D-printed models: a comparative study.
abstract: Background Accurate orbital volume (OV) measurement is essential for the management of orbital fractures. However, no consensus exists regarding the optimal method for OV assessment. Manual computed tomography (CT) planimetry remains the most widely used technique in clinical practice. Methods This study aimed to develop a direct method for measuring OV using 3D-printed orbital models and to compare it with manual CT planimetry in healthy orbits. Eighteen healthy orbits were analyzed. OV measurements were obtained using two direct-filling techniques on 3D-printed models: sand filling (3D-Orb-1) and water filling (3D-Orb-2). The results were compared with manual CT planimetry (Plani-Orb). Reproducibility was assessed using intraclass correlation coefficients, and agreement between methods was evaluated using linear regression and Bland-Altman analysis. Results Mean OV values were 23.34 ± 2.15 cm 3 for 3D-Orb-1, 23.31 ± 2.17 cm 3 for 3D-Orb-2, and 24.10 ± 2.37 cm 3 for Plani-Orb. Reproducibility was excellent for all methods, with ICC values of 0.963, 0.990, and 0.987 for 3D-Orb-1, 3D-Orb-2, and Plani-Orb, respectively. Strong correlations were observed between CT planimetry and both sand-filling ( R 2 = 0.823; P < 0.0001) and water-filling techniques ( R 2 = 0.798; P < 0.0001). Bland-Altman analysis demonstrated good agreement between methods. Conclusion The 3D-printing-assisted OV measurement method is reliable, reproducible, and cost-effective for orbital volumetric assessment in both clinical and preclinical experimental settings. This technique may serve as a valuable tool for validating computer-assisted OV measurement algorithms and for the in vitro evaluation of orbital implants and medical devices.

title: Intraoperative pneumothorax during arthroscopic rotator cuff repair: a case report and literature review.
abstract: Introduction and importance Arthroscopic rotator cuff repair is generally safe, but intraoperative pneumothorax is a rare, potentially fatal complication with poorly defined mechanisms and limited clinical guidance. This report aims to clarify the clinical course, mechanisms, and management of this complication, highlighting novel intraoperative warning signs and actionable prevention strategies. Case presentation A 50-year-old female with a full-thickness right supraspinatus tear underwent arthroscopic repair in the left lateral position under general anesthesia with an interscalene nerve block. Preoperative pulmonary function and chest imaging were normal. Intraoperatively, abrupt oxygen desaturation (SpO 2 to 79%), reduced tidal volume (500 → 332 mL), and elevated inspiratory pressure (9→18 cmH 2 O) developed near the completion of the procedure. Chest radiography confirmed a right pneumothorax with 70% lung collapse. A closed thoracic drain was emergently placed upon completion of the surgery. The patient recovered uneventfully, with drain removal on postoperative day 2 and discharge on day 7. Three-month follow-up confirmed full rotator cuff healing and normal pulmonary status. Clinical discussion Intraoperative pneumothorax in shoulder arthroscopy arises from a multifactorial mechanism: barotrauma from high pump pressure, pleural micro-perforation, and anesthetic-related airway pressure elevation. title: Liver resection for xanthogranulomatous cholecystitis: justified intervention or over treatment dilemma - a case series and review of literature.
abstract: Background Xanthogranulomatous cholecystitis (XGC) is a rare inflammatory gallbladder disease that frequently mimics gallbladder carcinoma (GBC). This clinical and radiological resemblance often results in extensive surgical resections for an ultimately benign condition, leading to avoidable patient morbidity. Objective To review the clinical presentations and radiological features of patients with histologically proven XGC who underwent radical surgery for suspected GBC and to identify factors that may help reduce unnecessary extended resections. Methods This retrospective case series analyzed data from patients at our institution from January 2008 to December 2023. We reviewed demographic data, clinical features, imaging, operative details, and outcomes for consecutive patients with a final diagnosis of XGC who underwent radical or extended resections for presumed malignancy. Results Eight patients underwent extended resections. All experienced right hypochondrial pain, while weight loss (50%) and jaundice (25%) were observed. Carbohydrate antigen 19-9 levels were consistently normal in six patients and borderline elevated in two patients. Imaging revealed gallbladder wall thickening in 100% of cases and radiologic invasion into adjacent organs in 87.5%. Intraoperatively, dense fibrosis and apparent local infiltration were universal findings. Following radical surgery, postoperative complications occurred in 50% of patients. Final histopathology confirmed XGC in all cases, with no evidence of malignancy. Conclusion While radical surgical resection remains a clinical necessity in diagnostically ambiguous cases, the primary paradigm for hepatopancreatobiliary surgeons must shift toward optimization. Incorporating advanced modern imaging, including AI-assisted radiomics, to accurately differentiate XGC from GBC, alongside mandatory intraoperative frozen-section analysis is imperative to mitigate the risk of severe overtreatment while preserving oncological efficacy.

title: Role of platelet to lymphocyte ratio to predict complicated acute appendicitis: a prospective observational cross-sectional study.
abstract: Background Ultrasonography and computed tomography are reliable for diagnosing acute appendicitis, but they are costly, time-consuming, and often unavailable in resource-limited settings. They also require skilled personnel to perform and interpret the studies. Hence, there is a growing need for simpler, more accessible, and reliable diagnostic alternatives. Numerous markers and scoring tools have been proposed, but many lack adequate sensitivity and specificity for distinguishing between uncomplicated and complicated appendicitis. Therefore, identifying a reliable tool with high diagnostic accuracy remains a key focus of ongoing research. This study aims to evaluate the ability of the platelet-to-lymphocyte ratio (PLR) to differentiate between complicated and uncomplicated appendicitis. Methods A prospective observational cross-sectional study was conducted at our institution from January to October 2024. PLR was analyzed in 116 patients diagnosed with acute appendicitis. Based on intraoperative findings, patients were categorized into uncomplicated and complicated appendicitis groups. PLR values were compared between the groups, and a receiver operating characteristic curve was generated. Sensitivity and specificity were calculated, and the optimal cut-off was determined using Youden's index. Results Among 116 patients (57 males and 59 females), complicated appendicitis was more common in females (57.4%) than males (42.6%). The highest proportion of complicated cases (34%) occurred in patients aged ≥50 years. The area under the curve was 0.924 with a standard error of 0.026. The maximum Youden's index (0.709) was observed at a PLR value of 162.2, which was identified as the optimal cut-off, yielding a sensitivity of 72.3% and a specificity of 98.6% for differentiating complicated from uncomplicated appendicitis. Conclusion This study showed a significant association between PLR and complicated appendicitis.

title: Rapidly destructive "dry" infectious spondylitis caused by methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus argenteus in an immunosuppressed patient with Crohn's disease.
abstract: Introduction Although Staphylococcus aureus is a well-known pathogen, infectious spondylitis caused by methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus argenteus is exceedingly rare. We report a unique case of rapidly progressive vertebral collapse caused by this pathogen in a patient with Crohn's disease (CD), highlighting the diagnostic challenges and successful surgical management. Case presentation A 68-year-old woman with a long-standing history of CD treated with azathioprine presented with progressive low back pain and bilateral lower-extremity radicular pain. Initial computed tomography revealed collapse of the first lumbar vertebral body without definite paraspinal abscess formation, leading to an initial diagnosis of an osteoporotic compression fracture. Despite conservative treatment, the patient's condition rapidly deteriorated, resulting in severe kyphotic deformity and neurological deficits consistent with conus medullaris syndrome. Discussion Intraoperative findings demonstrated extensive vertebral osteolysis and dense fibrotic tissue without macroscopic purulence, consistent with a "dry" infection. Tissue cultures confirmed infectious spondylitis caused by methicillin-resistant S. argenteus . A single-stage combined surgical approach was performed, consisting of posterior instrumentation from T10 to L4 followed by anterior corpectomy and reconstruction using an expandable titanium cage via a retroperitoneal approach. Conclusion This case suggests that infectious spondylitis caused by methicillin-resistant S. argenteus may present as a rapidly destructive yet clinically subtle infection in immunosuppressed patients with CD. Early clinical suspicion and timely surgical stabilization combined with appropriate antimicrobial therapy, may lead to favorable outcomes, even in high-risk patients with delayed diagnosis.
