title: Management of Monochorionic Twins: A Comprehensive Review of Major Guidelines.
abstract: Importance Monochorionic (MC) twin pregnancies are at risk of unique fetal and obstetric complications, which require increased surveillance and specific interventions to minimize the associated neonatal morbidity and mortality. Objective This review aimed to evaluate and compare the most recently published influential guidelines on the management of monochorionic twin pregnancies. Evidence acquisition A comparative review of guidelines from the Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists (RCOG), the Society of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists of Canada (SOGC), the Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists (RANZCOG), the International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics (FIGO), and the International Society of Ultrasound in Obstetrics and Gynaecology (ISUOG) was carried out. Results All the reviewed guidelines recommend the determination of chorionicity and amnionicity in the first trimester, along with the precise labeling of the twins and confirmation of the gestational age based on the crown-rump length of the larger twin or the dates of assisted reproductive techniques. They also encourage the performance of aneuploidy screening during the first trimester, using either a combined nuchal translucency and biochemical markers test or cfDNA. A detailed anatomy scan is recommended, with emphasis on the fetal cardiac assessment. There is agreement on the recommended ultrasonographic surveillance protocol, the diagnostic criteria of TTTS, TAPS, and TRAP, the optimal timing of delivery in case of uncomplicated MC twins, and the need for earlier delivery in case of complications or MCMA twins. All the reviewed medical societies provide similar recommendations regarding the management of pregnancies complicated by TTTS, TAPS, discordant fetal anomaly, and demise of one co-twin. Minor discrepancies were identified regarding the diagnosis and management of sFGR, the routine assessment of cervical length, as well as the first-line aneuploidy screening method. Conclusions Multiple pregnancies pose significant maternal, fetal, and obstetric risks compared with singleton pregnancies, with MC twins being at the highest risk of adverse perinatal outcomes, particularly in the absence of increased surveillance or therapeutic interventions. The development and implementation of consistent international evidence-based practice guidelines for the prompt diagnosis and management of MC twin pregnancies and their associated complications may contribute to more favorable outcomes.

title: Radiographic union rate and predictors of nonunion after primary surgical implant generation network intramedullary nailing for open tibial shaft fractures at a major trauma center in Ethiopia.
abstract: Open tibial shaft fractures are a major source of morbidity in low- and middle-income countries, yet outcome data after Surgical Implant Generation Network (SIGN) intramedullary nailing (IMN) remain few. The study aimed to determine the radiographic union rate and identify predictors of nonunion after primary SIGN IMN for Gustilo-Anderson (GA) grade I through IIIA open tibial shaft fractures at a large trauma center in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia. A retrospective cross-sectional study was conducted at AaBET Hospital, reviewing records and radiographs of patients treated between July 2016 and July 2022. Radiographic union was assessed at minimum 1 year using the Radiographic Union Scale for Tibial Fractures (RUST). Associations between clinical variables and union were analyzed with Fisher exact test, Mann-Whitney U test, and binary logistic regression. Eighty-seven patients met inclusion criteria (mean age 32.9 years; 86.2% male). Road traffic accidents accounted for 78.2% of injuries. The radiographic union rate was 89.7% (78 of 87). On multivariable analysis, GA grade IIIA (odds ratio [OR]: 36.2; 95% confidence interval [CI]: 4.21-90; P = 0.013), postoperative infection (OR: 20.2; 95% CI: 2.15-189; P = 0.023), and surgical delay beyond 48 hours (OR: 16.5; 95% CI: 1.88-144; P = 0.009) were independently associated with nonunion. Primary SIGN IMN yielded a high union rate for GA I to IIIA open tibial shaft fractures in this low- and middle-income countries setting. GA grade, postoperative infection, and delay to surgery were the principal barriers to union. These findings support early surgical intervention and rigorous infection control in resource-limited settings. Prognostic Level IV.

title: Sudden Unexpected Perinatal Death Due to Undiagnosed Diffuse Placental Chorioangiomatosis.
abstract: Chorioangiomatosis is a rare placental vascular disorder that may lead to severe fetal compromise and, in exceptional cases, sudden perinatal death. Its prenatal diagnosis remains challenging because diffuse lesions may lack a discrete placental mass and escape routine ultrasonographic detection. We report a case of sudden unexpected neonatal death occurring immediately after delivery following an apparently uncomplicated full-term pregnancy. External and macroscopic internal postmortem examinations were unremarkable. Histological evaluation revealed signs of chronic intrauterine hypoxia, while placental examination demonstrated diffuse chorioangiomatosis characterized by widespread capillary proliferation within immature chorionic villi and vascular wall hypertrophy. These findings supported a diagnosis of placental insufficiency leading to fatal hypoxia. This case highlights the critical role of placental histopathology in the forensic investigation of perinatal deaths, particularly when routine autopsy findings are negative. It also underscores the limitations of prenatal imaging in detecting diffuse placental vascular lesions. Recognition of this entity is essential to avoid misclassification of death and to ensure appropriate medico-legal assessment.

title: The 2026 World Health Organization Classification of Tumors of Soft Tissue and Bone: 6th Edition.
abstract: The 6th edition of the World Health Organization Classification of Soft Tissue and Bone Tumors (STB6) integrates the latest scientific and molecular discoveries with decades of pathological expertise to establish a globally accepted common language for diagnosis and clinical behavior. In this volume, the "essential" and "desirable" diagnostic criteria have been refined, considering different resource settings, ensuring accuracy while maintaining flexibility. A tumor type (entity) is a tumor in which multiple parameters (eg, clinical, histopathological, and/or genetic features) differ from those of other tumor types. In total, 19 new entities met these criteria and were added. A subtype is different in at least one dimension from the main tumor type (clinical, histopathological, or genetic), preferably resulting in a different treatment or outcome. A morphological pattern (no longer "variant") is important for pathologists to be aware of to facilitate recognition but is not associated with different clinical behavior. The classification was drafted by 203 editors and authors from 27 countries, representing genetics, medical oncology, surgical oncology, orthopedic surgery, and radiology, in addition to pathology. STB6 includes soft tissue tumors (n=116), bone tumors (n=46), vascular tumors of soft tissue and bone (n=18), undifferentiated spindle and round cell sarcomas (n=4), hematopoietic and dendritic cell neoplasms (n=6), and genetic syndromes (n=6). In total, 62 sarcomas are included. A consensus was reached among the expert editorial board. In this review, we highlight changes in tumor classification in STB6, including recently described tumor types, novel diagnostic markers, recent discoveries in molecular genetics, and improvements in prognostication.

title: Artificial Intelligence Segmentation In Musculoskeletal Ultrasound: A Novel Study Across Five Joints Using Expert Ground Truth.
abstract: Objective To evaluate the performance of an artificial intelligence (AI) technology in recognizing and segmenting anatomical structures across five joints (shoulder, elbow, wrist/hand, knee, and ankle/foot) in musculoskeletal ultrasound (US). Design This cross-sectional study included 79 adults. Software segmentations were compared to ground truth annotations provided by four experts. Performance was assessed using positive predictive agreement (PPA) and negative predictive agreement (NPA), with a true/false threshold defined as a dice similarity coefficient (DSC) ≥0.50. Subjects with and without sonographic disorders were evaluated to assess robustness. Results 3017 cine clips (15600 frames) covering 120 anatomical structures were analyzed. PPA and NPA exceeded 0.90 for most structures; tendons, muscles, and nerves showed near-perfect agreement (≥0.97). Similar performance was observed in healthy subjects (PPA: 0.93-0.96; NPA: 0.94-0.99) and subjects with sonographic disorders (PPA: 0.91-0.96; NPA: 0.91-0.99) (P<0.001). Conclusion This first large-scale study demonstrates the high accuracy and reliability of AI-based segmentation. By improving anatomical identification consistency during image acquisition, the software may help reduce technical operator dependency. The results further indicate strong potential for real-time assistance, supporting clinicians and trainees, and underscore the broader applicability of AI-based software in musculoskeletal US.

title: Diagnostic Accuracy of Ultrasound for Localizing Lymphovenous Anastomosis Sites in Lymphedema Surgery.
abstract: Background Preoperative vessel mapping is critical for successful lymphovenous anastomosis (LVA) in supermicrosurgical lymphedema treatment. Indocyanine green lymphography is common but limited by poor depth penetration and reduced visibility in advanced disease. This study aimed to evaluate the diagnostic accuracy, measurement agreement with intraoperative findings, and procedural efficiency of preoperative ultrasound in identifying surgically compatible LVA sites. Methods This study retrospectively analyzed prospectively collected data between April 2019 and January 2024 at a secondary care center. Consecutive patients with scintigraphically confirmed limb lymphedema underwent preoperative ultrasound to localize LVA sites, with intraoperative findings as the reference standard. Diagnostic accuracy was assessed using positive predictive value (PPV), Bland-Altman analysis, multivariable logistic regression, and subgroup testing. Results Eighty-seven patients (mean age, 55.8 ± 12.8 years; 75 women) underwent 109 ultrasound examinations. Of 470 ultrasound-localized sites, 285 were selected for surgery; 272 were intraoperatively confirmed (PPV, 95.4%; 95% CI: 92.3, 97.5%). The 13 false positives were independent of tissue thickness, vessel size, depth, and distance (all p > 0.17). Ultrasound diameters showed minimal bias compared with intraoperative measurements [+0.13 mm (95% CI: 0.09, 0.17) for lymphatics; -0.10 mm (95% CI: -0.17, -0.04) for veins]. Mean total examination time was 34.7 ± 9.6 minutes; per-image analysis averaged 7.2 ± 2.3 minutes and was unrelated to diagnostic accuracy (p = 0.74). Conclusions Preoperative ultrasound enabled accurate, reproducible localization of LVA sites with strong anatomical agreement and consistent performance across participant and anatomical variables.

title: Alpha1-Antitrypsin Mitigates Radiation-Induced Capsular Contracture and Fibrosis In-Vivo.
abstract: Introduction Capsular contracture remains a significant complication after alloplastic breast reconstruction, particularly following post-mastectomy radiotherapy. This study evaluated the therapeutic potential of human alpha-1 antitrypsin (hAAT) in reducing radiation-associated capsular fibrosis. Methods Textured silicone-discs were implanted subcutaneously in female C57BL/6 mice on day 0, followed immediately by localized 15 Gy irradiation of the implantation site. Mice were assigned to non-irradiated controls, irradiated albumin-treated controls, or irradiated hAAT-treated groups. Albumin control or hAAT was administered locally on days 0, 3, and 6. Capsule formation was assessed by MRI on day 21. Explants were collected on days 14 and 21 for histology, and day-21 tissues were further analyzed by gene expression profiling of inflammatory and fibrotic mediators. Human dermal fibroblasts were used to assess hAAT effects on radiation-associated TGFβ expression in vitro. Result Irradiated controls developed significant capsule thickening, disorganized collagen deposition, and inflammatory infiltration compared with non-irradiated controls. In contrast, hAAT-treated irradiated mice demonstrated capsule thickness comparable to non-irradiated controls, with improved extracellular matrix organization and reduced inflammation. hAAT treatment reduced interleukin-1 beta (IL-1β), transforming growth factor beta (TGFβ), and collagen type I expression, increased the interleukin-1 receptor antagonist/interleukin-1 beta (IL-1Ra/IL-1β) ratio, and upregulated Sloan-Kettering Institute proto-oncogene (SKI) expression, resulting in predominance of SKI over TGFβ compared with irradiated controls. In a separate in-vitro human dermal fibroblast model, hAAT attenuated radiation-induced TGFβ upregulation. Conclusion Local hAAT treatment may reduce early radiation-associated peri-silicone inflammation and fibrotic capsule formation, supporting its further investigation as a prophylactic strategy in implant-based reconstruction.

title: Daily Peer Review Reduces Replanning and Activity-Based Costs in a Network of Community Radiation Oncology Centers.
abstract: Background and objectives Peer review of radiation therapy plans is an essential quality assurance process; however, when performed after the initial treatment plan has already been created, it can lead to avoidable replanning, delays, and increased resource utilization. In this study, we implemented a quality improvement initiative to reduce the rate of replanning and utilize time-driven activity-based costing (TDABC) to measure its impact. Methods Plan-Do-Study-Act was utilized to move peer review from after treatment planning to before treatment planning at a network of freestanding cancer centers. Chart rounds were shifted from once-weekly retrospective plan review to daily prospective peer review of physician contours and prescriptions before dosimetric planning, immediately followed by a structured multidisciplinary clinical huddle (including physicians, nurses, dosimetrists, physicists, therapists, patient schedulers, medical assistants, and benefit representatives) to address care coordination. The rate of monthly dosimetry replans and their causes were abstracted from the electronic medical record system for 1 year before and after the initiative. TDABC was calculated for the cost of the replanning workflow, for the cost of the baseline once-weekly chart rounds, and for the cost of daily chart rounds. Results Four thousand five hundred seventy-two new treatment starts were observed over the 25-month period (average of 175.9 per month), of which 393 (8.6%) were replans. Before the change in peer review, the average monthly replan rate was 11.1%, which declined rapidly to 6.9% after the intervention. The most common reasons for replans included volume segmentation (33%), imaging and closer inspection (30%), and change in tumor (13%). Average fully loaded TDABC cost per replan occurrence was $908; weekly cost of once-weekly chart rounds was $3249; and weekly cost of daily chart rounds (4 days per week) was $4300. The reduction in replans translated to $118,996 in saved costs during the 14-month period ($8499 per month), with a net TDABC savings of $4294 to the practice per month or $60,124 for the 14-month postintervention timeframe. Conclusions Physician-related peer review of contours and medical decision-making in the context of a daily chart rounds can lead to a reduction in the number of replans and reduction in resource utilization. With the movement towards value-based care, an understanding of both outcomes and sources of costs to the provider is essential.

title: Beyond the usual suspects: a rare case report of left anterior descending artery to pulmonary artery fistula with concomitant atherosclerotic coronary artery disease.
abstract: Introduction Coronary artery fistulas (CAFs) are rare vascular anomalies that may remain asymptomatic or present with symptoms mimicking coronary artery disease (CAD). In individuals with coexisting coronary atherosclerosis, fistulas that originate from the left anterior descending artery (LAD) and end in the pulmonary artery are extremely rare and can complicate the clinical picture. Case presentation A 46-year-old man, an ex-smoker with a previous non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction, presented with worsening chest pain and dyspnea. Coronary angiography demonstrated severe left anterior descending artery (LAD) stenosis, diagonal artery occlusion, and a fistulous communication arising from the proximal LAD with focal aneurysmal dilatation draining into the main pulmonary artery. Cardiac computed tomography (CT) confirmed multiple fistulous tracts between the LAD and the pulmonary artery. Following a multidisciplinary discussion, the patient underwent surgical fistula ligation with double-vessel coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG). The postoperative course was uneventful, with complete symptom resolution at six-month follow-up. Discussion The coexistence of an LAD-pulmonary artery fistula with significant CAD is rare and poses diagnostic and therapeutic challenges. For precise anatomical delineation and surgical planning, multimodality imaging was crucial. Surgical ligation of the fistula, combined with CABG, allowed definitive treatment of both pathologies in a single procedure. Conclusion This case highlights the importance of considering CAFs as a potential coexisting pathology in adults presenting with angina and coronary artery disease. Recognition of such anomalies is essential to guide appropriate management and prevent complications.

title: On-top plasty for late-presenting atypical Wassel type VII thumb duplication: a case report.
abstract: Background Thumb duplication beyond early childhood presents unique reconstructive challenges. On-top plasty offers an alternative when standard excision may yield suboptimal results. Case presentation We report a 10-year-old girl with late-presenting bilateral thumb duplication. The right hand demonstrated atypical Wassel type VII configuration with a floating ulnar thumb and hypoplastic radial triphalangeal thumb. On-top plasty was performed, combining the distal ulnar segment with the proximal radial segment. At 6-month follow-up, radiographic union was achieved with good functional outcomes including pinch and grasp activities. Clinical discussion Wassel type VII thumb duplication presents significant reconstructive challenges, especially when anatomical dominance is indistinct. Although early intervention is recommended, late presentation necessitates strategies that account for established skeletal maturation and functional adaptation. Simple excision was considered insufficient for achieving optimal stability and esthetics. Therefore, on-top plasty was performed, combining the most robust distal and proximal components. A proximal phalanx-level osteotomy enabled preservation of native thenar insertions and collateral ligament stability, which are essential for stable opposition and pinch mechanics. This case demonstrates that individualized, anatomy-based reconstruction using on-top plasty can overcome the limitations of delayed presentation, yielding satisfactory outcomes despite advanced age at presentation. Conclusion On-top plasty represents a viable reconstructive option for complex thumb polydactyly in late-presenting cases when neither duplicated digit offers adequate functional potential.

title: From surgery to immediate function: fixed screw-retained corticobasal® implant-supported prostheses with multi-unit abutments: a case report.
abstract: Introduction Edentulism remains a global oral health problem, compromising oral health and adversely affecting patient's esthetics, chewing, speech, and quality of life. Appropriate treatment planning and meticulous implant and prosthetic selection are vital to treatment success. Evidence has documented higher survival rates for Corticobasal ® cement-retained implant-supported prosthetic designs. However, there is limited literature regarding screw-retained Corticobasal ® implant-supported prostheses utilizing multi-unit abutments with longitudinal follow-up. This report describes two cases of immediately loaded, screw-retained Corticobasal ® implant-supported prostheses with multi-unit abutments and a 24-month follow-up period. Case presentation We present a multidisciplinary treatment approach for two cases presenting with complete and partial edentulism, rehabilitated with immediately loaded, screw-retained, fixed single-piece Corticobasal ® implant prostheses with multi-unit abutments and a 2-year follow-up period of 2 years. The reported cases showed 100% implant survival, along with healthy peri-implant soft tissues, improved speech, chewing ability, esthetics, self-esteem, and superior patient satisfaction. Clinical discussion The use of screw-retained multi-unit abutments highlighted the advantages of retrievability, facilitating easy removal for maintenance, repair, or access for hygiene, especially in full-arch replacement cases, which often favor multi-unit abutment systems. This treatment approach demonstrated favorable peri-implant soft-tissue conditions and satisfactory prosthetic outcomes during the observation period, in line with the literature. Conclusion Within the limitations of this two-patient case series, immediately loaded, screw-retained Corticobasal ® implant-supported prostheses utilizing multi-unit abutments demonstrated favorable clinical and radiographic outcomes over a 24-month follow-up period. This treatment approach provided predictable function, stable peri-implant health, and significant improvements in mastication, speech, appearance, and overall satisfaction. Larger prospective studies with longer follow-up are required to validate these findings.

title: Revision surgery for gastric conduit volvulus and siphon formation after abdominothoracic esophagectomy: a case report.
abstract: Introduction and importance Ivor Lewis esophagectomy is a complex procedure associated with a wide range of complications, including anastomotic leakage, fistula formation, and strictures. While many of these complications can be managed endoscopically, revision surgery is rarely required. This case report describes the management of therapy-refractory stricture symptoms following Ivor Lewis esophagectomy, necessitating surgical revision and reconfiguration of the gastric conduit. Case presentation We report a 58-year-old male patient who underwent a totally robotic Ivor Lewis esophagectomy for Barrett's dysplasia 4 years earlier at another institution. This patient was initially treated for a confirmed esophageal stenosis due to achalasia with multiple pneumatic dilatations (2007-2009) and a laparoscopic myotomy in 2015. Due to Barrett's dysplasia, our patient underwent a robotic Ivor Lewis esophagectomy in 2021 at another institution. At presentation, the patient's BMI was 23.1 kg/m 2 (weight 74 kg and height 179 cm). The patient was a non-smoker, did not use recreational drugs, and drank alcohol occasionally. The patient's medical history included arterial hypertension, for which he was taking two antihypertensive medications. No allergies were reported. Diagnostic evaluation, including computed tomography, revealed volvulus of the gastric conduit with supradiaphragmatic siphon formation. Surgical revision with reconfiguration to achieve upright positioning of the gastric conduit was performed. Clinical discussion We believe that adequate conduit length optimization and tension-free positioning are critical in preventing this complication. Potential causes of gastric conduit volvulus include intraoperative conduit malrotation, excessive conduit length, overly proximal anastomotic positioning, outlet obstruction due to a narrow hiatus or pyloric dysfunction, and vagal denervation. In the present case, a low intrathoracic anastomosis resulted in excessive conduit length, predisposing to fixation at the right hemidiaphragm and subsequent siphon formation, leading to functional stenosis. Conclusion Thoracic revision surgery after abdominothoracic esophagectomy is technically demanding, but it was unavoidable in this case. Endoscopic treatment options are limited in the presence of gastric conduit volvulus. Shortening an excessively long gastric conduit following Ivor Lewis esophagectomy represents a safe and effective surgical option.

title: Primary colonic lymphoma as an uncommon cause of large bowel obstruction: a case report.
abstract: Introduction and importance Primary colonic lymphoma (PCL) is a rare extranodal manifestation of non-Hodgkin lymphoma, accounting for a small fraction of colorectal malignancies. Due to its low incidence and nonspecific clinical and radiological features, PCL is frequently misdiagnosed as colonic adenocarcinoma. Optimal management remains poorly defined, and current treatment strategies rely on retrospective data and expert consensus. Case presentation We report the case of a 69-year-old woman who presented with right lower quadrant abdominal pain and was found to have a near-obstructing ascending colon mass with extensive regional and retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy on computed tomography. Colonoscopic biopsies were nondiagnostic despite a malignant-appearing lesion. Given impending obstruction, the patient underwent an open right hemicolectomy with primary anastomosis. Histopathologic and immunohistochemical analysis of the surgical specimen revealed diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL). Postoperative staging with positron emission tomography demonstrated fluorodeoxyglucose-avid nodal disease. The patient was treated with adjuvant immunochemotherapy and radiotherapy, achieving a complete metabolic response on follow-up imaging. Clinical discussion This case highlights the diagnostic challenges of PCL and emphasizes the importance of surgical resection in symptomatic patients for both definitive diagnosis and management. DLBCL is the most common PCL subtype and responds favorably to multimodal therapy, including rituximab, cyclophosphamide, hydroxydaunorubicin, oncovin, prednisone-based chemotherapy. Positron-emission tomography-computed tomography plays a critical role in staging and assessment of treatment response. Conclusion PCL should be considered in the differential diagnosis of colonic masses, particularly when biopsy results are inconclusive. A multidisciplinary, multimodal treatment approach can lead to favorable outcomes. Further prospective studies are needed to establish standardized management guidelines.

title: Real-time CT-MRI fusion intraoperative navigation during laparoscopic ultra-low anterior resection for low rectal cancer: a case report.
abstract: Background Laparoscopic ultra-low anterior resection (uLAR) remains technically challenging due to limited visualization and difficulty identifying dissection planes in the distal pelvis. Image-guided navigation has emerged as a potential tool to enhance intraoperative precision. Case presentation A 52-year-old man with low rectal adenocarcinoma located 3 cm from the anal verge underwent laparoscopic uLAR with total mesorectal excision assisted by real-time computed tomography-magnetic resonance imaging (CT-MRI)-based intraoperative navigation. The patient had no significant comorbidities and had received neoadjuvant therapy. The navigation system enabled accurate tumor localization and facilitated dissection within the correct mesorectal plane in a technically demanding pelvic environment. The procedure was completed without intraoperative complications. Discussion Navigation-assisted surgery provided enhanced anatomical orientation and continuous spatial feedback during deep pelvic dissection, particularly in the presence of tissue edema and distorted anatomy. This approach may reduce the risk of positive margins and improve preservation of critical pelvic structures. Conclusion Real-time CT-MRI-based intraoperative navigation is a feasible and safe adjunct in complex rectal surgery. This approach may be particularly valuable in anatomically challenging pelves or post-neoadjuvant settings.

title: Hammock-like placental appearance associated with amniotic sheet: a rare case report.
abstract: Introduction and importance Amniotic sheets are uncommon intrauterine membranous structures that arise from uterine synechiae and may alter placental morphology and implantation. Although generally considered benign, placental attachment to an amniotic sheet can mimic abnormal placental invasion disorders, pose diagnostic challenges, and potentially lead to unnecessary obstetric interventions. Case presentation We report the case of a 35-year-old gravida four, para two woman who presented at 36 weeks and 4 days of gestation with labor pains and vaginal bleeding. Prenatal ultrasound and magnetic resonance imaging revealed a posterior placenta intersected by a thick, transverse amniotic sheet, creating a hammock-like placental appearance and raising suspicion for placenta accreta. Due to a history of prior cesarean section and abnormal placentation, a cesarean delivery was performed. A healthy male neonate was delivered. Intraoperative findings confirmed placental adhesion to the amniotic sheet without evidence of deep placental invasion. Both maternal and neonatal outcomes were favorable. Clinical discussion Placental implantation on an amniotic sheet may closely resemble placenta accreta spectrum disorders on imaging, particularly in the presence of prior uterine surgery. Careful interpretation of prenatal imaging, combined with awareness of this rare entity, is essential to avoid misdiagnosis and overtreatment. Conclusion This case highlights that amniotic sheets with placental attachment can mimic abnormal placental invasion on prenatal imaging. Accurate recognition of this condition is crucial for appropriate surgical planning and may help prevent unnecessary radical interventions while ensuring optimal maternal and fetal outcomes.

title: Irreducible inguinoscrotal hernia containing cecum and inflamed appendix: an unusual variant of Amyand's hernia managed with Lichtenstein mesh repair - a case report.
abstract: Introduction Amyand's hernia occurs in approximately 0.1-1.7% of all inguinal hernias. Concurrent cecal herniation is a rare variant, reported only in isolated case reports and not documented as a distinct category in large systematic reviews. Management in resource-limited settings, particularly in patients with metabolic comorbidities, is sparsely reported in the literature. Presentation of case A 46-year-old man with chronic alcohol use presented with a 6-month history of irreducible right inguinoscrotal swelling. Examination revealed a 12 × 8 cm pyriform mass. Laboratory findings indicated alcohol-related hepatic dysfunction and thrombocytopenia. Surgical planning was guided by ultrasonography in the absence of computed tomography (CT). Intraoperative findings confirmed a Losanoff-Basson Type 2 Amyand's hernia with concurrent cecal herniation; an appendectomy and Lichtenstein mesh repair were performed. Postoperative alcohol withdrawal necessitated ICU admission. Discussion Concurrent cecal herniation with Amyand's hernia can be identified clinically and by ultrasonography when CT is unavailable. Mesh repair can be performed in Losanoff-Basson Type 2 cases without peritoneal contamination, as supported by emerging literature. A multidisciplinary approach can manage alcohol-related metabolic comorbidity. Conclusion Amyand's hernia with concomitant cecal herniation is a rare surgical case. Individualized decision-making regarding appendectomy and mesh use and systematic management of alcohol-related comorbidities are essential for favorable outcomes in resource-limited settings.

title: Ascending colon volvulus with a transmesocolic hernia in a young adult: a case report.
abstract: Introduction Volvulus of the cecum and ascending colon represents a rare but critical etiology of acute intestinal obstruction. It likely results from a congenital failure of fusion of the colon to the parietal peritoneum during embryogenesis and may be associated with other anatomical anomalies, such as congenital mesocolic defects. Presentation of case An 18-year-old man presented with a 4-day history of progressive abdominal pain localizing to the right iliac fossa, associated with nausea and vomiting. Despite inconclusive but abnormal findings on computed tomography, persistent signs of an acute abdomen led to surgical exploration. Intraoperative findings revealed a volvulus of the cecum and ascending colon caused by congenital malrotation with absent lateral peritoneal attachments of the large bowel, along with internal herniation of small-bowel loops through a large congenital defect in the mesocolon. The volvulus was detorsed, the herniated small-bowel loops were reduced, and the defect was closed primarily. Conclusion This case highlights the diagnostic difficulty of congenital anomalies in adults, as symptoms are often nonspecific and insidious. Given the rarity of such presentations in adulthood, a high index of clinical suspicion is essential.

title: Granular cell tumor of the vocal cord: a case report.
abstract: Introduction and importance Granular cell tumors (GCTs) are uncommon, typically benign neoplasms of Schwann cell origin. Although the head and neck region remains the most common site, laryngeal involvement is rare, accounting for only 3-10% of GCTs. Recognizing laryngeal GCTs is crucial because their subtle clinical presentation and potential to histologically mimic malignancy represent a significant diagnostic challenge. Case presentation A 40-year-old woman with a 30 pack-year smoking history presented with a 3-year history of progressive dysphonia. Laryngoscopic examination revealed a whitish, pedunculated, exophytic mass located on the posterior third of the left vocal cord. Histopathology showed a benign mesenchymal proliferation of large, polygonal cells with finely granular, eosinophilic cytoplasm beneath an unremarkable squamous epithelium with no dysplasia or pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia. Clinical discussion The primary diagnostic challenge with laryngeal GCTs is distinguishing them from malignancies - particularly squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) - and from other soft tissue tumors. In this case, immunohistochemistry was essential for a definitive diagnosis. The tumor cells demonstrated diffuse positivity for S-100 protein, confirming their Schwann cell origin, and they were negative for desmin and myogenin, which successfully excluded myogenic neoplasms and SCC. Conclusion Although rare, laryngeal GCTs should be considered in the differential diagnosis of vocal cord lesions causing chronic dysphonia. Accurate histopathological and immunohistochemical evaluation is essential to avoid misdiagnosis and potential overtreatment. Complete endoscopic excision offers an excellent prognosis, although long-term surveillance is recommended.

title: Surgical release of a deep retro-equatorial band in congenital unilateral restrictive strabismus: a case report.
abstract: Introduction and importance Congenital unilateral restrictive strabismus may result from anomalous orbital tissue, extraocular muscle abnormalities, or congenital cranial dysinnervation. Forced duction testing can identify a passive mechanical component, but does not establish tissue identity or exclude coexisting dysinnervation. Presentation of the case An 11-year-old girl had congenital ocular misalignment with 40 prism diopters (PD) of right hypotropia, 20 PD of exotropia, and left supraduction and infraduction each graded -3, with full abduction and adduction. Apparent right upper-eyelid asymmetry was formally evaluated by the oculoplastic service and diagnosed as pseudoptosis associated with the right hypotropia rather than true ptosis; margin reflex distance-1 was 3 mm bilaterally with each eye fixating, and levator function was >14 mm bilaterally. Computed tomography showed intact orbital walls without obvious extraocular muscle entrapment; dedicated orbital magnetic resonance imaging was not performed. Under general anesthesia, multidirectional forced duction testing demonstrated no appreciable restriction during passive elevation in adduction. Maximum resistance was localized to a focal central point in the superior plane, while passive infraduction and horizontal rotations were unrestricted. Superior exploration identified a focal tissue attachment at the nasal aspect of the normal-appearing superior rectus region and, more posteriorly, a deep retro-equatorial band. Stepwise release markedly improved passive elevation, although mild residual superior restriction remained because further posterior dissection was limited by the risk to deep orbital neurovascular structures and the optic nerve. No tissue was submitted for histopathological examination. A 10 mm left lateral rectus recession was performed for the associated exotropia. At 12 months, horizontal alignment was orthotropic, and residual right hypotropia measured 12 PD at distance and approximately 8-10 PD at near. Left supraduction and infraduction had both improved to approximately -2, while abduction and adduction remained full. Clinical discussion The intraoperative response supports an important mechanical contribution, although the identity, full posterior extent, and anatomical relationships of the abnormal tissue remain uncertain. The documented diagnosis of pseudoptosis with preserved levator function, rather than true congenital ptosis, makes classic congenital fibrosis of the extraocular muscles (CFEOM)1 and CFEOM2 less characteristic; however, CFEOM3 cannot be excluded without dedicated orbital/cranial nerve imaging and, when indicated, genetic assessment. Residual vertical motility limitation may reflect the safely unreleased posterior restriction, coexisting extraocular muscle dysplasia or dysinnervation, or a combination of these factors. Conclusion Stepwise partial release of a deep retro-equatorial band substantially reduced the accessible passive restriction while avoiding unsafe posterior dissection. At 12 months, vertical alignment and both supraduction and infraduction had improved, although residual right hypotropia and vertical motility limitation persisted. The findings support an important mechanical component but do not establish the precise tissue identity or exclude coexisting congenital dysinnervation.

Computed tomography showed intact orbital walls without obvious extraocular muscle entrapment; dedicated orbital magnetic resonance imaging was not performed. Under general anesthesia, multidirectional forced duction testing demonstrated no appreciable restriction during passive elevation in adduction. Maximum resistance was localized to a focal central point in the superior plane, while passive infraduction and horizontal rotations were unrestricted. Superior exploration identified a focal tissue attachment at the nasal aspect of the normal-appearing superior rectus region and, more posteriorly, a deep retro-equatorial band. Stepwise release markedly improved passive elevation, although mild residual superior restriction remained because further posterior dissection was limited by the risk to deep orbital neurovascular structures and the optic nerve. No tissue was submitted for histopathological examination. A 10 mm left lateral rectus recession was performed for the associated exotropia. At 12 months, horizontal alignment was orthotropic, and residual right hypotropia measured 12 PD at distance and approximately 8-10 PD at near. Left supraduction and infraduction had both improved to approximately -2, while abduction and adduction remained full.

Clinical discussion

The intraoperative response supports an important mechanical contribution, although the identity, full posterior extent, and anatomical relationships of the abnormal tissue remain uncertain. The documented diagnosis of pseudoptosis with preserved levator function, rather than true congenital ptosis, makes classic congenital fibrosis of the extraocular muscles (CFEOM)1 and CFEOM2 less characteristic; however, CFEOM3 cannot be excluded without dedicated orbital/cranial nerve imaging and, when indicated, genetic assessment. Residual vertical motility limitation may reflect the safely unreleased posterior restriction, coexisting extraocular muscle dysplasia or dysinnervation, or a combination of these factors.

Conclusion

Stepwise partial release of a deep retro-equatorial band substantially reduced the accessible passive restriction while avoiding unsafe posterior dissection. At 12 months, vertical alignment and both supraduction and infraduction had improved, although residual right hypotropia and vertical motility limitation persisted. The findings support an important mechanical component but do not establish the precise tissue identity or exclude coexisting congenital dysinnervation.

title: One-stage pancreaticoduodenectomy for penetrating pancreaticoduodenal trauma without preoperative computed tomography: a case report.
abstract: Introduction and importance Combined pancreaticoduodenal injuries after penetrating trauma are rare and life-threatening. The decision between damage-control surgery and a one-stage pancreaticoduodenectomy remains challenging. Presentation of the case A 37-year-old man presented with hemorrhagic shock after an occupational impalement injury. Because of hemodynamic instability and ongoing upper gastrointestinal bleeding, emergency laparotomy was performed without preoperative computed tomography. Intraoperatively, a destructive injury involving the pancreatic head and the second portion of the duodenum was identified, with associated gastric perforations and a liver laceration. Clinical discussion Primary repair with drainage was considered insufficient for definitive management because of the combined destructive pancreaticoduodenal injury, persistent bleeding, the proximity to the periampullary region, and the inability to reliably exclude injury to critical periampullary ductal structures. After hemorrhage control and continued resuscitation, blood pressure and heart rate remained stable without recurrent hypotension or vasopressor requirements. Based on these intraoperative clinical findings, a one-stage, non-pylorus-preserving pancreaticoduodenectomy with reconstruction was performed. Conclusion One-stage emergency pancreaticoduodenectomy may be feasible in carefully selected patients with destructive penetrating pancreaticoduodenal trauma when hemorrhage has been controlled and intraoperative clinical assessment supports definitive reconstruction by an experienced hepatopancreatobiliary team.

title: Surgical management of splenic artery aneurysms: a case series of three patients with diverse presentations.
abstract: Background Splenic artery aneurysm (SAA) is the most common visceral artery aneurysm and includes true aneurysms and pseudoaneurysms, which have different etiologies and clinical behavior. Presentation ranges from incidental detection to life-threatening rupture with hemoperitoneum. Management depends on aneurysm size, symptoms, morphology, anatomical relationships, comorbidities, and rupture status. Methods We retrospectively described three consecutive patients with SAA or pseudoaneurysm treated surgically at a tertiary surgical center, Loghman Hakim Hospital, Shahid Beheshti University of Medical Sciences, Tehran, Iran, between 2020 and 2025. Clinical records, imaging, operative findings, histopathology, postoperative course, and available follow-up were reviewed. The series was reported in accordance with the PROCESS 2025 reporting guideline. Case presentations Case 1 was a 66-year-old man with chronic liver disease and thrombocytopenia in whom a giant true SAA measuring approximately 72 × 68 × 76 mm was incidentally identified during trauma imaging. The aneurysm was adjacent to the pancreatic body without rupture. Elective open splenectomy with aneurysm resection and concurrent liver wedge biopsy was performed. Case 2 was a 63-year-old woman with a 7-month history of postprandial epigastric pain and a symptomatic true SAA of undocumented size. Elective open resection with splenectomy was performed; histopathology unexpectedly demonstrated necrotizing granulomatous splenitis. Case 3 was a 38-year-old woman with sickle cell disease who developed acute abdominal pain after a generalized seizure, with severe anemia and hemoperitoneum. A ruptured splenic artery pseudoaneurysm was identified at emergency laparotomy after a ruptured ectopic pregnancy had initially been suspected. Results All three patients underwent open splenectomy with aneurysm excision, which was elective in cases 1 and 2 and emergent in case 3. There were no intraoperative deaths or reoperations. All three patients had uneventful postoperative recoveries. 6-month follow-up was available for case 1; longer-term uniform follow-up was not available for all patients. Conclusion SAAs encompass a broad clinical spectrum, from incidentally discovered giant aneurysms to symptomatic lesions and catastrophic rupture. These cases illustrate the importance of anatomy-directed treatment selection, early recognition of rupture, and consideration of vascular causes in patients with unexplained hemoperitoneum. Endovascular therapy is preferred for anatomically suitable elective lesions, whereas open surgery remains an important option for giant, complex, or ruptured aneurysms. The proposed algorithm is an educational synthesis of published evidence, current Society for Vascular Surgery guidelines recommendations, and the clinical experience represented by this institutional series rather than a prospectively validated decision tool.

title: Beyond the groin: a retroperitoneal liposarcoma with an unusual presentation: a case report.
abstract: Background Retroperitoneal liposarcoma is an uncommon malignancy that can present with aberrant manifestations and can sometimes resemble an inguinal hernia, creating diagnostic difficulties. Presentation of case We describe the case of a 52-year-old man who presented with a long-standing right inguinal swelling that was initially thought to be an inguinal hernia. Computed tomography with contrast enhancement showed a sizable retroperitoneal mass that extended into the inguinal canal, which was suspicious for malignancy. An exploratory laparotomy revealed a retroperitoneal tumor that followed the inguinal canal. Complete surgical excision was performed. A diagnosis of well-differentiated liposarcoma was established by histopathological and immunohistochemical analyses. The patient was referred for adjuvant radiotherapy and is in clinically stable condition, with no recurrence on follow-up. Discussion Retroperitoneal liposarcomas are often asymptomatic and may grow to a considerable size before diagnosis. They rarely invade the inguinal canal and resemble more common benign pathologies, including inguinal hernias, which may delay proper intervention. Conclusion This case highlights the importance of considering retroperitoneal malignancy in patients with atypical or non-reducible inguinal masses. Early imaging, correct diagnosis, and proper oncologic surgical planning are crucial to maximizing patient outcomes.

title: Dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans with fibrosarcomatous transformation of the abdominal wall: a case report and literature review.
abstract: Introduction and importance Dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans (DFSP) is a rare, locally aggressive cutaneous sarcoma. Its fibrosarcomatous variant (FS-DFSP) is an uncommon, high-grade subtype associated with increased risks of recurrence and metastasis. Case presentation A 43-year-old woman presented with a left iliac fossa skin mass evolving over 20 years, recently characterized by ulceration and bleeding. Computed tomography showed a well-defined anterior abdominal wall mass, initially mimicking a desmoid tumor. Biopsy suggested leiomyosarcoma or FS-DFSP; staging workup was negative. The patient underwent complete en bloc resection under general anesthesia. Histopathology confirmed fédération nationale des centres de lutte contre le cancer (FNCLCC) grade 2 FS-DFSP (70% FS component), staged pT2. The immunohistochemical study showed diffuse labeling of tumor cells across both components for CD34, with no staining for smooth muscle actin and caldesmon. Postoperative recovery was uneventful. Due to close margins (3 mm) near the iliac bone, adjuvant radiotherapy was administered (60 Gy, 2 Gy/day, 5 days per week). No recurrence occurred at the 2-year follow-up. Clinical discussion FS-DFSP poses diagnostic challenges due to nonspecific clinical and radiological features, requiring histopathological and immunohistochemical confirmation. While complete surgical excision is the cornerstone of treatment, adjuvant radiotherapy helps reduce the risk of local recurrence in cases with close or positive margins. Conclusion Managing FS-DFSP requires precise staging, clear margins, and a multidisciplinary consensus, including adjuvant radiotherapy when anatomical constraints limit surgical margins.

title: Gastric outlet obstruction caused by an impacted intramural gastric stone mimicking malignant pyloric stenosis: a case report.
abstract: Introduction Gastric cancer is among the leading causes of gastric outlet obstruction (GOO) in adults. We report an extremely rare case of GOO caused by an impacted intramural gastric stone mimicking malignant pyloric stenosis. Case presentation A 91-year-old man presented with nausea and reduced oral intake. Non-contrast computed tomography (CT) revealed marked gastric dilatation and a localized hyperdense lesion within the pyloric wall. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy revealed an elevated pyloric lesion that made endoscopic passage difficult. Although biopsy revealed no evidence of malignancy, intraoperative findings showed an inflammatory mass involving the pylorus and gallbladder fundus. Because gallbladder invasion by gastric cancer could not be excluded, distal gastrectomy with cholecystectomy was performed. Histopathological examination revealed an impacted intramural stone within the pyloric wall with marked fibrosis and inflammatory changes causing pyloric stenosis. The gallbladder showed adenomyomatosis with multiple gallstones. The intramural stone and gallbladder stones had similar compositions, suggesting a possible pathogenetic relationship. Case discussion Preoperative differentiation from malignant pyloric stenosis was difficult. However, a localized hyperdense lesion within the pyloric wall on CT may provide an important diagnostic clue. Since intramural gastric stones are benign, alternative treatments other than gastrectomy may be considered when a preoperative diagnosis is established. Conclusion Awareness of this rare entity may facilitate preoperative diagnosis and the selection of appropriate treatment when malignancy can be reasonably excluded.

title: Comparison and Combination of Radiomics, Deep Learning, and Subjective Assessment for Differentiating Immature and Mature Ovarian Teratomas on Abdominal CT.
abstract: Objective Preoperatively, ovarian teratomas are often misclassified into immature and mature types, potentially resulting in adverse clinical outcomes. This study compared the diagnostic accuracy of radiomics-based machine learning (ML), deep learning (DL), and subjective radiologic assessment for differentiating immature from mature ovarian teratomas on abdominal computed tomography (CT) and evaluated whether combining these approaches improves discrimination. Methods We retrospectively reviewed imaging data of 31 cases with pathologically confirmed immature teratomas and 61 age- and size-matched cases of mature teratomas (mean age=18.1±9.2 y vs. 20.9±10.0 y). Two radiologists independently annotated predefined CT features to construct a multivariable logistic regression model. Radiomics features were extracted from precontrast CT with 3 masks: whole tumor, calcification, and fat. Radiomics models were developed using 4 ML pipelines (logistic regression, random forest, support vector machine, and neural network). DL models were constructed with a 3D-ResNet18 on full-volume and tumor-segmented CT, with and without transfer learning (TL). A combined model was constructed by averaging their calibrated predicted probabilities. The diagnostic performance was assessed by the mean area under the receiver-operating characteristic curve (AUC). Results In the full cohort, the 4 individual approaches performed similarly, with overlapping CIs: wavelet-transformed precontrast radiomics 0.820 (95% CI: 0.798-0.841), precontrast radiomics 0.817, subjective assessment 0.814, and DL 0.810. Combining them outperformed every individual approach (0.865; ΔAUC: 0.045, 95% CI: 0.032-0.060; Holm-adjusted P<0.001). Among the 81 tumors containing calcification, where calcification-mask radiomics could also be evaluated, all approaches performed better, and the combined model again outperformed each of them (0.891; ΔAUC: 0.035), as did the combined model among the 90 tumors containing fat (0.872; ΔAUC: 0.047; both P<0.001). Conclusion Radiomics shows moderate performance in CT-based discrimination between immature and mature ovarian teratomas, with subjective radiologic assessment and DL performing at a comparable level. Combining the 3 consistently outperformed anyone alone, indicating that quantitative image analysis complements rather than replaces expert visual interpretation and may help reduce preoperative misclassification.

title: Whole-Body MRI of Inflammatory and Infectious Musculoskeletal Diseases: Emphasis on Chronic Nonbacterial Osteomyelitis and Systemic Inflammatory Disorders.
abstract: Whole-body magnetic resonance imaging (WBMRI) has emerged as the primary imaging tool for multifocal inflammatory and infectious musculoskeletal diseases. By extending coverage from the vertex to the toes in a single, radiation-free examination, WBMRI enables the detection of clinically occult lesions, disease-specific pattern recognition across bone marrow, joints, entheses, and muscles, and objective monitoring of disease activity and treatment response. This review describes the WBMRI findings-with detailed imaging features and distribution patterns-in chronic nonbacterial osteitis, SAPHO syndrome, seronegative spondyloarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, juvenile idiopathic arthritis, polymyalgia rheumatica, idiopathic inflammatory myopathies, and fever of unknown origin, with emphasis on validated quantitative scoring tools, disease-specific acquisition protocols, and structured reporting strategies for the practicing radiologist. WBMRI provides unique clinical value by mapping total lesion burden, supporting differential diagnosis, identifying biopsy targets, and tracking treatment response. Disease-specific protocols-tailored to the pathophysiological target of each condition-are essential for maximizing diagnostic yield. Quantitative scoring tools and advanced MRI sequences may improve the characterization of disease burden and longitudinal assessment.

title: Size and Attenuation Measurements for Urinary Stone on Virtual Monoenergetic Images Derived From Dual Layer Spectral CT: A Phantom Study.
abstract: Objective This study aimed to investigate the optimal energy level for virtual monoenergetic (VM) images with specific window settings for stone size and attenuation measurements, and to determine the effects of radiation dose and reconstructed slice thickness on these measurements. Methods Forty-eight urinary calcium oxalate stones (<1 cm in diameter) were placed within a 32-cm phantom, and CT scans were performed on a dual-layer detector scanner at 3 radiation doses (volumetric computed tomography dose index=5, 10, and 15 mGy). Images were reconstructed as conventional 120-kVp and VM images ranging from 40 to 100 keV in 10-keV increments with a slice thickness of 1 mm. In addition, 70-keV images were reconstructed at slice thicknesses of 2 and 5 mm. Length, width, and attenuation were measured at bone and soft tissue window settings by 2 radiologists. The reference stone size was measured with a digital caliper, and the reference attenuation was measured on 120 kVp images. Statistical analyses were performed using the paired t test, the Wilcoxon test, and repeated-measures one-way analysis of variance. Results The stone size and attenuation decreased with increasing energy level of the VM images, irrespective of window settings. The stone size on the VM 70- to 90-keV images under the soft tissue window and on the VM 40-keV images under the bone window was closest to the true size. Attenuation values measured on the VM 70-keV images were similar to those obtained on the conventional 120-kVp images across both window settings. In addition, measurements of stone size (length and width) and attenuation on VM images with thinner slices were closer to the true value. Conclusions For VM images used to measure urinary stone size and attenuation, the optimal energy level required may differ based on the window settings. In addition, reconstructed thinner slice thickness can improve measurement accuracy.

The reference stone size was measured with a digital caliper, and the reference attenuation was measured on 120 kVp images. Statistical analyses were performed using the paired t test, the Wilcoxon test, and repeated-measures one-way analysis of variance.

Results

The stone size and attenuation decreased with increasing energy level of the VM images, irrespective of window settings. The stone size on the VM 70- to 90-keV images under the soft tissue window and on the VM 40-keV images under the bone window was closest to the true size. Attenuation values measured on the VM 70-keV images were similar to those obtained on the conventional 120-kVp images across both window settings. In addition, measurements of stone size (length and width) and attenuation on VM images with thinner slices were closer to the true value.

Conclusions

For VM images used to measure urinary stone size and attenuation, the optimal energy level required may differ based on the window settings. In addition, reconstructed thinner slice thickness can improve measurement accuracy.

title: AI-Assisted Lung Segmentation for Lung Transplant Volumetry: Effect of Radiation Dose Reduction.
abstract: Objective Accurate lung volumetry is essential for donor-recipient size matching in lung transplantation. This study evaluated the impact of radiation dose reduction on the robustness of AI-based whole-lung segmentation, 5-lobe segmentation, and automated tissue classification. Methods Fifty cases from the Cancer Image Archive (TCIA) Low-dose CT Image and Projection Data set were analyzed. A reduced-dose data set at 10% of the routine dose for each case was generated using validated projection-domain noise insertion. Whole-lung and 5-lobe segmentation were performed using the Lung CT Segmenter module with the lungmask deep learning model in 3D Slicer. Segmentation accuracy was quantified using the Dice similarity coefficient (DSC), 95th percentile Hausdorff distance (HD95), and maximum Hausdorff distance (HDmax). Automated tissue classification and volumetry were performed using the Lung CT Analyzer module. Results Whole-lung segmentation demonstrated excellent consistency between full-dose and 10% dose images (mean DSC 0.997±0.002, HD95 0.73±0.26 mm). In contrast, 5-lobe segmentation showed substantially lower accuracy and greater variability, even at routine dose. Automated tissue classification revealed a mean decrease in functional (inflated) lung volume of 17.12%±5.69% in the right lung and 17.15%±5.56% in the left lung, accompanied by marked increases in emphysema, infiltrated, and collapsed volumes. Conclusion AI-based whole-lung segmentation remains highly accurate at 10% of the routine dose, supporting its potential for lung transplant volumetry. However, tissue classification and 5-lobe segmentation exhibited notable degradation, highlighting limitations of existing tools at ultra-low dose levels.

title: Preoperative Contrast-Enhanced CT-Based Three-Dimensional Fractal Analysis of Automatically Segmented Tumors for Predicting PD-L1 Expression in Hepatocellular Carcinoma: A Preliminary Study.
abstract: Objectives To evaluate whether 3-dimensional fractal features extracted from automatically segmented hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) tumor volumes on preoperative contrast-enhanced CT (CECT) can predict programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) expression. Methods This retrospective study included patients with pathologically confirmed HCC between January 2022 and March 2026 who underwent multiphasic liver CECT and PD-L1 immunohistochemical staining of surgical or biopsy tumor specimens. PD-L1 positivity was defined as a combined positive score ≥1. Patients were randomly divided into training and validation cohorts. Tumor VOIs were automatically segmented on portal venous phase CECT using the uAI Research Portal. Three-dimensional fractal dimension (FD3D) and 3-dimensional lacunarity (Lac3D) were extracted using the box-counting method. LASSO logistic regression was used to select predictors of PD-L1 positivity and to build a combined model. Results A total of 134 patients with HCC were included, of whom 69 had PD-L1-positive tumors, and 65 had PD-L1-negative tumors. Patients were randomly assigned to the training cohort (n=87; 44 PD-L1-positive) and validation cohort (n=47; 25 PD-L1-positive). In both cohorts, tumor FD3D and Lac3D were significantly higher in PD-L1-positive patients than in PD-L1-negative patients (both P<0.05). LASSO-logistic regression identified FD3D, Lac3D, and radiologic venous invasion (RVI) as predictors of PD-L1 positivity. The combined model incorporating these variables showed good predictive performance in the validation cohort, with an AUC value of 0.813. Calibration curves and decision curve analysis demonstrated good model calibration and clinical net benefit. Conclusion Tumor 3-dimensional fractal features derived from preoperative CECT can quantitatively reflect the spatial structural complexity and heterogeneity of HCC. A combined model integrating FD3D, Lac3D, and RVI may facilitate noninvasive preoperative prediction of PD-L1 expression and serve as an imaging biomarker for characterizing tumor immune-related features.

title: Reduced Lumbar Lordosis in Fibromyalgia: Radiographic Evidence of Lumbar Straightening by L1-L5 Cobb Angle.
abstract: Background Reduced lumbar lordosis has been observed in patients with low back pain, but lumbar straightening has not been well characterized in fibromyalgia. We hypothesized that fibromyalgia would be associated with reduced lumbar curvature on standing radiographs. Objective To evaluate lumbar lordosis, quantified by the L1-L5 Cobb angle, in patients with fibromyalgia compared with patients with other rheumatic diseases and low back pain. Design Retrospective, cross-sectional observational study. Setting Rheumatology office practice. Participants A consecutive series of 245 patients aged 18 to 70 years who underwent lumbar spine radiography for moderate-to-severe low back pain between 2012 and 2014 was reviewed. Of these, 164 patients met American College of Rheumatology criteria for fibromyalgia and 81 met criteria for another rheumatic disease, including rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis, or polymyalgia rheumatica. Intervention Not applicable. Main outcome measures Lumbar lordosis was measured on standing lateral lumbar spine radiographs using the Cobb angle between the superior endplate of L1 and inferior endplate of L5. The prevalence of a nearly straight lumbar spine, defined as a Cobb angle ≤10 degrees, and more complete straightening, defined as a Cobb angle ≤5 degrees, was also assessed. Results Mean L1-L5 Cobb angle was significantly lower in patients with fibromyalgia than in rheumatic disease controls (15.2±12.2 degrees vs. 23.3±13.4 degrees, respectively; p <0.001). A Cobb angle ≤10 degrees was present in 72 (44%) patients with fibromyalgia compared with 17 (21%) controls (p <0.001). A Cobb angle ≤5 degrees was present in 42 (26%) patients with fibromyalgia compared with 5 (6%) controls (p <0.001). Limitations The study was retrospective and conducted at a single site. Both groups consisted of patients referred for lumbar imaging because of low back pain, and no asymptomatic healthy control group was included. Potential confounding factors, including body mass index, age, sex, pain duration, and medication use, were not formally analyzed. Conclusion Patients with fibromyalgia had significantly reduced lumbar lordosis and a higher prevalence of near-complete lumbar straightening than patients with other rheumatic diseases referred for lumbar imaging due to low back pain. Because lumbar straightening was also present in the comparator group, it is not specific enough to serve as a standalone diagnostic sign. Lumbar lordotic straightening may represent an additional radiographic observation associated with fibromyalgia and warrants prospective investigation, including evaluation of its potential relationship with paraspinal muscle tension. Primary funding source This research was privately funded and received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors. Trial registration Not applicable.

title: Metal Artifact Reduction in Lumbar Spine Instrumentation: A Comparison of Photon-Counting Detector-Computed Tomography Versus Energy-Integrating Detector-Computed Tomography, Iterative Metal Artifact Reduction, and Virtual Monoenergetic Imaging in 100 Examinations.
abstract: Objective Photon-counting detector (PCD) computed tomography (CT) systems allow the reconstruction of virtual monoenergetic images (VMIs) from inherently available spectral data. However, qualitative and quantitative evaluations of VMI in combination with tin-prefiltration (Sn) and iterative metal artifact reduction (iMAR), as well as their comparison to energy-integrating detector (EID) CT, are limited; therefore, the objective was to compare their performance qualitatively and quantitatively in the setting of lumbar spine instrumentation. Materials and methods Retrospectively, 100 clinical Sn CT scans after lumbar spine fusion surgery (50 EID and 50 PCD) were analyzed. Metal artifacts were quantitatively and qualitatively assessed in EID standard (EID std ), PCD standard (PCD std ), and PCD VMI at 120 keV (PCD VMI120 ), PCD iMAR (PCD iMAR ), and combined PCD VMI at 120 keV + iMAR (PCD VMI120+iMAR ). Regions of interest were placed in the most hyperdense and hypodense areas near metal artifacts, and the attenuation and SD/noise (SD) of Hounsfield Units (HU) were assessed as a quantitative artifact surrogate. For qualitative evaluation, 2 independent readers rated 6 image features on a 4-point Likert Scale. Results Seventy-four patients were included, of whom 26 underwent both an EID and a PCD CT. Radiation doses were significantly lower ( P < 0.01) for PCD CT [median CTDIvol of 6.4 mGy (4.6 to 8.4)] compared with EID CT [median CTDI vol of 12.5 mGy (11.1 to 13.7)]. Hypodense artifact attenuation was significantly reduced ( P < 0.01) with PCD iMAR (HU -260), PCD VMI120 (-176), and PCD VMI120+IMAR (-60) compared with EID std (-626). Hyperdense artifact attenuation was significantly reduced ( P < 0.01) in PCD VMI120 (HU 103) and PCD VMI120+IMAR (-1) compared with EID std (577). Qualitative artifact extent was rated significantly less severe in PCD iMAR and PCD VMI120+iMAR images compared with EID std ( P ≤ 0.01), while trabecular and cortical bone visibility was rated lower in PCD iMAR (2.73) and PCD VMI120 (2.63), P < 0.01, and lowest in PCD VMI120+iMAR (1.82) compared with EID std (3.19), P < 0.01. Significantly ( P < 0.01) more silhouette artifacts were present in the 100 kVp subgroup compared with the 140 kVp subgroup in PCD VMI120 and PCD VMI120+iMAR , and significantly ( P < 0.01) more dark zone artifacts in the PCD VMI120 series at 100 kVp compared with 140 kVp. Conclusion PCD CT with VMI 120 or iMAR achieved artifact reduction comparable to EID CT for lumbar spine metal artifact reduction, at nearly half the radiation dose. Combining VMI120 + iMAR provided the strongest qualitative and quantitative artifact reduction, but at the cost of the lowest cortical and trabecular bone visibility. 140 kVp acquisitions should be favored over 100 kVp acquisitions in PCD to reduce the occurrence of "dark zone" and "silhouette artifacts", suggesting a fixed tube voltage instead of an automatic tube voltage setting in instrumented lumbar spine imaging. VMI reconstruction of tin-filtered lumbar spine CT effectively reduces metal artifacts, with PCD favored over EID for its inherent spectral capabilities and the potential for substantial dose reduction.

title: Photon-counting Detector CT Spectral Reconstructions for Radiomics-based Liver Lesion Classification: A Multicenter Study.
abstract: Objectives Accurate noninvasive classification of hepatic lesions remains a diagnostic challenge, particularly on conventional CT. Photon Counting Detector CT (PCD-CT) offers spectral imaging capabilities that may enhance tissue characterization. This study aimed to evaluate the performance of radiomics-based machine learning for differentiating benign and malignant liver lesions using multispectral virtual monochromatic and material decomposition images derived from contrast-enhanced PCD-CT. Materials and methods This multicenter study included patients with focal hepatic lesions, scanned on PCD-CT at 2 separate institutions. Lesions were automatically segmented by a nnU-Net model and confirmed by an abdominal radiologist. Volumetric segmentations were used to extract radiomic features from 9 spectral datasets: 40, 50, 70, 90, 110, 140, and 180 keV, virtual non-contrast (VNC), and iodine density maps (IDM). A patient-based classification analysis was conducted by training multiple machine-learning models, with lesion-level predictions aggregated per patient. A Random Forest model further evaluated classification performancef across all train-test reconstruction combinations. Results The cohort comprised 378 patients (median age: 62; 59.5% female) from 2 centers, including 190 benign (n=227 lesions) and 188 with malignant (n=2681 lesions) hepatic findings. Random forest model trained on VNC achieved highest performance [AUC: 0.899; 95% CI (0.840-0.951); Accuracy 83.5%). In the cross-domain analysis, all training reconstructions achieved similar mean AUCs (0.75 to 0.83). Evaluation performance varied across test levels. Models tested on 110, 140, and 180 keV, and VNC showed the highest stability (median AUC ≥ 0.83), while 40 keV, 50 keV, and IDM resulted in lower and more variable AUCs (median AUC ≤ 0.71). Conclusion Radiomics-based machine learning enables reliable differentiation between malignant and benign hepatic lesions on PCD-CT. The choice of test reconstruction influenced performance: higher energy levels and VNC images yielded more stable results. Incorporating high-energy reconstructions and VNC images into radiomic workflows for liver lesion risk stratification may enable noninvasive triage and reduce the need for invasive diagnostics.

title: Improved Visualization of Heart Valves With 4D-CT Using a Novel Motion Correction Algorithm.
abstract: Objective Motion artifacts remain a limitation of cardiac CT when assessing both native and prosthetic heart valves, particularly during phases of rapid motion. This may lead to reduced image quality, potentially impairing the evaluation of valvular movement and pathology. The purpose of this study was to evaluate whether a novel reconstruction-based motion correction algorithm improves image quality and reduces motion artifacts of native and prosthetic heart valves compared with standard reconstructions in photon-counting detector CT (PCD-CT). Materials and methods In this retrospective single-center study, 57 patients [21 women; median age, 71 (interquartile range, 57 to 78 y)] who underwent clinically indicated 4D cardiac CT for suspected native and prosthetic valvular disease were included. Images were acquired using retrospectively electrocardiography (ECG)-gated spiral dual-source PCD-CT without ECG-pulsing. Images were reconstructed in 10% steps throughout the RR-interval using both standard (TrueStack) and an otherwise identical reconstruction using the novel motion correction algorithm (ZeeFreePlus). Subjective image quality and motion artifacts were independently assessed by 2 blinded, experienced readers using a 4-point visual analog scale for 3 categories: valve frame/annulus, valve leaflets, and valvular pathology. Objective analysis included quantification of the volume of artifacts throughout the cardiac cycle. Results A total of 68 valves were evaluated, including 57 prosthetic valves (22 transcatheter aortic valve replacements and 19 surgical valves, 11 mitral valves, and 5 tricuspid valve interventions) and 11 native valves. Valvular pathology was present in 29 cases, with the most prevalent being hypoattenuated leaflet thickening in 14/29 (48%). Motion-corrected reconstructions significantly improved image quality and reduced motion artifacts across all cardiac phases and all categories (all, P <0.001). The largest improvements were observed during systole, particularly at 10% of the RR-interval, with significantly greater gains than during diastole ( P <0.05). Improvements were consistent across aortic and atrioventricular prosthetic valves and translated into improved visualization of valvular pathology ( P <0.001). Objective quantitative analysis corroborated the subjective image quality findings by demonstrating reductions in the volumes of motion-induced artifacts when using the algorithm ( P <0.001). Conclusions A novel motion correction algorithm substantially reduced motion artifacts and improved image quality in both native and prosthetic heart valve imaging with PCD-CT, with the largest improvements in systole. These benefits resulted in enhanced visualization of valvular pathology, potentially reinforcing the growing clinical role of cardiac CT for the assessment of valve disease.

The largest improvements were observed during systole, particularly at 10% of the RR-interval, with significantly greater gains than during diastole ( P <0.05). Improvements were consistent across aortic and atrioventricular prosthetic valves and translated into improved visualization of valvular pathology ( P <0.001). Objective quantitative analysis corroborated the subjective image quality findings by demonstrating reductions in the volumes of motion-induced artifacts when using the algorithm ( P <0.001).

Conclusions

A novel motion correction algorithm substantially reduced motion artifacts and improved image quality in both native and prosthetic heart valve imaging with PCD-CT, with the largest improvements in systole. These benefits resulted in enhanced visualization of valvular pathology, potentially reinforcing the growing clinical role of cardiac CT for the assessment of valve disease.

title: A Head-to-Head Comparison of Detection Rate and Tumor Uptake of FAPI, PSMA, and FDG PET/CT in Newly Diagnosed High-risk Prostate Cancer.
abstract: This study was designed to investigate the detection rate and tumor uptake of 18F-AlF-NOTA-De-FAPI PET/CT in newly diagnosed high-risk prostate cancer (PCa), compared with 68Ga-PSMA-11 and 18F-FDG PET/CT. This study enrolled 48 patients with biopsy-diagnosed, treatment-naive high-risk PCa who underwent 18F-AlF-NOTA-De-FAPI, 68Ga-PSMA-11, and 18F-FDG PET/CT between April and December 2024. A head-to-head comparison of detection rate and tumor uptake was performed among the 3 tracers. In addition, 18F-AlF-NOTA-De-FAPI and 68Ga-PSMA-11 dual-tracer PET was used to characterize the imaging phenotypes of each lesion and interlesional heterogeneity. A total of 477 lesions were detected by the 3 PET tracers. 68Ga-PSMA-11 exhibited the highest overall detection rate (96.4%), followed by 18F-AlF-NOTA-De-FAPI (81.1%) and 18F-FDG (66.0%). A total of 17 68Ga-PSMA-11-negative lesions were identified in 8 patients, all of which were detected by 18F-AlF-NOTA-De-FAPI, whereas only 12 were detected by 18F-FDG. Combined 68Ga-PSMA-11 and 18F-AlF-NOTA-De-FAPI PET identified all lesions detected by triple-tracer PET. Based on relative tracer dominance of dual-tracer PET, patients were classified as PSMA-dominant (n=23), FAPI-dominant (n=5), or mixed phenotype (n=20). The mixed phenotype with marked interlesional heterogeneity might be associated with more advanced clinical characteristics, with a higher proportion of metastatic disease and a greater metastatic burden. 18F-AlF-NOTA-De-FAPI is a promising PET tracer for newly diagnosed high-risk PCa. It may improve the detection rate of 68Ga-PSMA-11-negative lesions and provide complementary information that could reflect interlesional heterogeneity. The clinical value of combining 18F-AlF-NOTA-De-FAPI and 68Ga-PSMA-11 PET requires further validation in larger prospective cohorts.

title: 177Lu-PSMA Therapy in Recurrent High-Grade Glioma: A Pilot Study With Dosimetric Insights.
abstract: Purpose Patients with recurrent high-grade glioma have poor prognosis and limited treatment options. This pilot study evaluated the feasibility and potential clinical benefit of 177Lu-PSMA therapy in this patient population. Patients and methods Eligible patients were selected for treatment based on positive 68Ga-PSMA-PET findings. 177Lu-PSMA (7.4 GBq/200 mCi) was administered at 6-8-week intervals and continued as long as well-tolerated. The safety, tolerability, and efficacy of 177Lu-PSMA were assessed in each treatment cycle using PET/MRI, SPECT/CT, blood tests, neurological tests, and patient-reported outcome measures. Results Ten patients were enrolled (WHO grade 4 glioblastoma, n=6; WHO grade 4 astrocytoma, n=1; WHO grade 3 astrocytoma, n=3). 68Ga-PSMA-PET before treatment demonstrated tumor uptake in 9 patients (median SUVmax: 6.4, IQR: 4.2-9.0). Six patients received treatment (20 cycles total; range: 1-7 per patient). Median absorbed dose per cycle was 0.9 Gy (IQR: 0.8-1.1) for tumors, 2.6 Gy (IQR: 1.9-3.2) for kidneys, and 1.7 Gy (IQR: 1.5-2.2) for parotid glands. No CTCAE grade 3-4 toxicities occurred. The most common patient-reported symptoms were fatigue, transient xerostomia, and nausea. Median survival from treatment initiation was 187 days (range: 87-756) and the median progression-free survival was 45 days (range: 41-335). MRI (RANO 2.0) demonstrated stable disease in half of the patients during all or part of the treatment course. Conclusions 177Lu-PSMA therapy was feasible and well-tolerated. Radiologic stabilization was observed in a subset of patients, but strategies to increase tumor dose delivery may be needed to improve efficacy.

Ten patients were enrolled (WHO grade 4 glioblastoma, n=6; WHO grade 4 astrocytoma, n=1; WHO grade 3 astrocytoma, n=3). 68Ga-PSMA-PET before treatment demonstrated tumor uptake in 9 patients (median SUVmax: 6.4, IQR: 4.2-9.0).
